candidates.name: Richard Pulcher
candidates.leg_q1: I was 19 years a union steward, Teamsters Local 662. I want to make WI worker friendly. I have served my community as a firefighter, first responder, and EMT basic. I am a Lutheran, ELCA. I support a woman's right to healthcare. If the healthcare provider determines an abortion is necessary, it should be a legal choice. I support cleaning the PFAS pollution wherever it exists. I have a BS degree in economics with supporting courses in history and quantitative analysis. I have worked as a laaborer, using my education as a union steward. I could have had a career in economics, But i chose to be a worker, fighting for workers rights.
candidates.leg_q2: The Bend Gold and Copper Mine. It is contained in a sulfide ore that turns into sulfuric acid when exposed to air and water. It is very near the Yellow River. Any spill could pollute the ground water, drinking water, and possibly the ground around it. In the 1990s the Wisconsin Legislature passed a 'Prove it First' mining law. It was repealed during the Walker Administration. I would support legislation passing some sort of the 'Prove it First' mining law.
candidates.leg_q3: There is a lack of respect for the "rule of law" by some local sheriff's departments. They ignore complaints about stealing campaign signs. They let some illegal activity pass without reporting.  While prosecuting others. This has happened in our local village. Law enforcement ignored my report of the village president having the village pay his delinquent sewer bill. The president then did other questional practices. Who in state government can a person call if the sheriff and district attorney ignore illegal activity. A system should be established that doesn't require suing the sheriff in the court where he charges other criminals. I believe no one should be above the law.
candidates.leg_q4: The Green Bay Packers are the only NFL team owned by local investors.

candidates.name: Charly Ray
candidates.elected_experience: Town Board member (10 years); chair (8 years); County Board (7 years)
candidates.leg_q1: Because I am passionate about a government in service of the people. I know the people and land of northwest Wisconsin and am ready to faithfully represent the community. I am a county supervisor, small business owner and forester. I am a listener, problem solver and negotiator who looks for creative ways to deliver better government. I believe in democracy, the Constitution, the rule of law and will stand up for our rights. I will work to address issues from the big picture — Badgercare buy-in for all — to small scale — reducing burdensome training requirements for volunteer EMS personnel. I will bring a real world common sense approach to Madison.
candidates.leg_q2: School funding. We need formula reform, voucher reform and bureaucracy reduction. The school funding formula from 1993 is overdue for revision. It’s not fair, especially to rural areas, causing disparities in costs to local schools and in tax burdens on local property owners. Vouchers shouldn’t be funded from school levies, but transition plans. Local tax bills should state the levy going to private schools. Private schools getting state aid should follow rules and reporting similar to public schools. Finally, vouchers should be systematically reduced with consideration for areas like Milwaukee where vouchers are filling a need. Difficult conversations about consolidation should be supported with creative solutions and funding to find solutions that work for our communities. We must reduce bureaucratic limits and burdens on schools.
candidates.leg_q3: Less bureaucracy and more service to the people. Less partisanship over serving the public good. Government should focus on real solutions to problems of everyday needs and mainstreet small businesses. Government is a tool for investment in our communities and we should treat it as such.
candidates.leg_q4: The Green Bay Packers are incorporated as a cooperative, owned by over 500,000 shareholders who vote on management policies.

candidates.name: Angie Sapik
candidates.elected_experience: Wisconsin State Assembly (2023-2025); Douglas County Board (2025-2026)
candidates.leg_q1: As a business professional, wife, and mother of two, I have experience in many facets of life that are headlining issues in politics. From lowering taxes to helping daycares survive so professional women can continue to thrive in the workplace, I understand the issues northern Wisconsinites face. My experience in the legislature and on the county board has helped me build relationships not just in my community, but throughout the state. We’ve funded our roads, given historic shared revenue increases, and I supported the coverage of 3D mammograms — reducing healthcare costs and saving lives. The work we have done sets the tone for the work we have yet to do, and I look forward to getting back to work for my constituents in the north.
candidates.leg_q2: The constant increase and instability of property taxes. The first thing is to get rid of the 402 year property tax increase under Evers administrations line-item veto. Wisconsinites deserve to know what to expect to pay for property taxes, and their bills should never shock them. The current administrations abuse of the line-item veto has to go.
candidates.leg_q3: Gov. Evers line item veto, increasing property taxes for 402 years, opened up a new discussion. With the advancement of AI, it's feasible for a bad government official to utilize an AI program to construct the state budget in a manner that suits him, rather than the people of Wisconsin the way it is intended. While I am a big fan of less government, we do need stronger safeguards against the influence of AI, and I believe getting rid of the line-item veto is important in protecting our budgeting and our agencies from manipulation.
candidates.leg_q4: Wisconsin has more lakes than Minnesota. Take that, Minnesota.

candidates.name: Dianne Hesselbein
candidates.elected_experience: Wisconsin State Senate (2023-present); Wisconsin State Assembly (2013-2023); Dane County Board (2008-2012);  Middleton Cross Plains Area School Board (2005-2008)
candidates.leg_q1: For the last 14 years, I have dedicated myself to serving the people, my friends and neighbors, in the 79th AD and 27th SD. Now, we are on the verge of retaking the Wisconsin State Senate for the first time in over a decade. From being in a super minority to now, I have advocated for my constituents, achieved fair maps, drafted legislation to regulate PFAS, and fought for women's right to access healthcare. 2026 presents us with a new opportunity. Instead of playing defense, I can focus on creating the change that people in the 27th District have been waiting for: free school meals for K-12 students, building affordable housing, and ensuring affordable access to quality healthcare.
candidates.leg_q2: As I’ve spoken to hundreds of constituents in the 27th SD, the issue I hear about most consistently is underfunded public education. Right now, the Middleton Cross Plains Area School District is weighing whether to place an operational referendum on the 2026 ballot. As with nearly all of the hundreds of referendums across Wisconsin for the last few years, this is not intended to enrich teachers or administrators, but to keep the doors open and ensure every child receives an adequate education. As we look forward to a Democratic majority, I pledge to work toward making up for lost dollars under Republican leadership. That starts with adjusting the funding formula, focusing on public rather than private education, and guaranteeing every K-12 student a free lunch.
candidates.leg_q3: As I have said before, a long-overdue adjustment is simply changing the faces at the table. For a decade, there have been entrenched voices that have acted as a bulwark against forward-thinking change. With new faces at the table, our range of legislative options opens up significantly. That being said, when we retake the majority, I intend to continue following the mantra, disagree without being disagreeable. We live in a state with diverse opinions, and respecting those who represent Wisconsinites who disagree with you is necessary to produce effective change.
candidates.leg_q4: A personal favorite centers on one of Wisconsin's most prolific legislators, Robert La Follette. As a Senator, he brought “the Wisconsin Idea” with him to Washington, D.C., specifically the State’s Legislative Reference Bureau, founded in 1901, which became the country's first agency dedicated to fact-finding and legislative research. In 1914, Senator La Follette led the effort to fund the creation of the Special Reference Unit within the Library of Congress, now known as the Congressional Research Service. His aspiration to promote informed legislators is the heartbeat of modern lawmaking.

candidates.name: Gillian Battino
candidates.leg_q1: I’m a retired physician and 20-year resident of Central Wisconsin. My family includes young adults, a sibling with a lifelong disability and elderly parents. I spent my career diagnosing, caring, and advocating for patients as they navigate the most difficult and life-threatening challenges. I’ve seen firsthand the direct impact of social and economic challenges on people’s lives. I know what happens when healthcare systems fail, roads crumble, and schools cannot provide for our children. I spent the last 10 years of my career working in Central and South America building healthcare infrastructure, educational programming, and quality assurances. I collaborate, team build, and I’ve witnessed the good and bad impact of legislation on people. I’m bold and collaborative. I know how to get things done.
candidates.leg_q2: Cost of living is the top issue. To address this, we need to make healthcare is affordable by expanding Medicaid and creating a public health insurance option so folks are not bankrupt by illness. We need to fully fund public schools, Public Safety and the maintenance of our roads and bridges so property taxes can go down and constant referenda stop. We need to close tax loopholes for wealthy corporations not paying their fair share yet rely on our hospitals, schools, and roads for their businesses and profits.
candidates.leg_q3: Republicans and Democrats must collaborate. The best policy is the result of collaboration between representatives with different backgrounds and opinions, but a common goal. I will work with anyone who wants to solve a problem for the people of Wisconsin. I will always put people before politics.
candidates.leg_q4: When I think of my home in central Wisconsin, I think of rolling hills, pristine lakes, fishing, wild turkey, deer, eagles, bear, marshes and birds. It is the most beautiful place on earth. I love that Earth Day began in Wisconsin shortly after I was born by Senator Gaylord Nelson. And I love that it is celebrated around the world today. I look forward to honoring that legacy with the preservation and protection of the natural beauty of Wisconsin.

candidates.leg_q1: My experience has proven to be a benefit to me as a former small business owner and my time in the legislature. As a lifelong resident of my district, I think I have a better than average knowledge of what matters to people living in western Wisconsin.
candidates.leg_q2: We recently suffered the closures of two hospitals in my district and access to the health care people need became preeminent to many families who may not have had that struggle before. We have made that the top area in which my office has been focused since those closures.
candidates.leg_q3: There is not enough space here to address how all the ways we should but I'll try. People have the right to know what ALL legislators offer. Currently, the majority party buries every bill offered by Democrats and never allows a public hearing including those bills. In the state Senate they don't have in-person executive hearings where we could debate bills and offer amendments. Bills are sent to our offices via paper ballot and we only vote in committee that way. In-person debate in the public eye matters.
candidates.leg_q4: One of the most famous stories from the Civil War is about the soldiers from Wisconsin that brought an Eagle into battle with them. The eagle Old Abe would circle the battlefield and return to the division after. After the war he was adopted by the legislature and lived in the Capitol until his death. A representative Old Abe is still perched in the Assembly chambers of Wisconsin. That eagle came from Eau Claire, my hometown, and Ol Abe is the mascot of one of our high schools.

candidates.name: Mike Van Someren
candidates.leg_q1: Voters who want a government focused on affordability, transparency, accountability, and enforcing the rules evenly should vote for me. I believe government should work like a fair referee: making sure families can afford a decent life, powerful interests play by the same rules as everyone else, and taxpayers know where their money is going. I’m not running to just talk about problems or wait for the perfect solution while families keep falling behind. I’m running to do something: to bring practical, accountable leadership to Madison, make progress where we can, and fight for working families who feel like the system is no longer built with them in mind.
candidates.leg_q2: The top issue is affordability. That includes groceries and gas, but it goes well beyond that. It’s property taxes, utility rates, housing, and most importantly, wages not keeping up with the cost of living. The first step is getting the market working again. That means reinvigorating antitrust enforcement so powerful companies cannot squeeze families, workers, and small businesses. It means limiting noncompete agreements to narrow situations where they are truly needed, not letting them trap workers in lower-wage jobs. It also means funding our priorities responsibly, instead of pushing costs onto local property taxpayers. And when we as taxpayers invest in private companies, those companies must perform. If they don’t, taxpayers should get their money back.
candidates.leg_q3: Wisconsin government should operate with more transparency, accountability, and focus that it had in the past. Too often, Madison debates slogans while families deal with the consequences including rising costs, underfunded priorities, and rules that apply differently depending on how much power somebody has. Government needs to be more practical. It should identify problems, set clear goals, measure whether policies are working, and be honest when they aren’t. It needs to stop pushing costs down to local communities and then blaming them for rising property taxes. It should also make sure that when taxpayer dollars are used to partner with private companies, the public gets a return on that investment. I don't believe government needs to be bigger or smaller. It just needs to work.
candidates.leg_q4: The University of Wisconsin-Madison's football field, Camp Randall, was actually a Civil War training grounds which was previously the state fair. Now it's a 76,000+ seat stadium.

candidates.name: Alicia Saunders
candidates.leg_q1: I'm a Navy veteran, a blue-collar worker, and a Fox Valley mom who knows what it's like to live paycheck to paycheck. I served on the flight deck of an aircraft carrier during Operation Iraqi Freedom, and I've spent the last two years fighting for my neighbors without a title or a paycheck: connecting veterans to housing and property tax help, and speaking up when local leaders ignored the people they serve. Assembly District 2 deserves a representative who lives the challenges working families face and shows up between elections, not just during them. I'll listen first, work across the aisle, and treat every constituent with respect, never as a talking point. I'm running to serve, not to build a career.
candidates.leg_q2: The rising cost of living and property taxes are at the heart of it. Property taxes keep climbing because the state has underfunded schools and shared revenue for years, forcing local governments to make up the difference on your tax bill. Madison shifts the cost, then blames local governments. I'd fight to restore real funding for our schools and municipalities so communities aren't forced to raise property taxes just to keep the lights on. I'd also protect ratepayers from out-of-state owned data centers that could shift billions onto our utility bills, and expand property tax relief for disabled veterans and seniors. Affordability comes down to whether the people already here can afford to stay.
candidates.leg_q3: Government should be transparent and accountable to the people, not the powerful. Too often, major decisions get rushed through like floor amendments dropped with no fiscal estimate, no committee review, no chance for the public to weigh in. That's how billions in giveaways slip past us. I'd push for honest fiscal transparency on every bill, so voters can see who pays and who benefits before a vote happens. I'd also restore the habit of governing for the long term instead of the next election. Representatives should show up between campaigns, hold real listening sessions, and put constituents ahead of donors and party leadership. People have lost trust in government because it stopped working for them. Earning it back starts with telling the truth.
candidates.leg_q4: My favorite is right here in Kimberly, where I live. The village is named after John A. Kimberly, a founder of Kimberly-Clark, and he had many of the homes built for the people who worked at the paper mill and their families. You can still spot them small, square, serviceable houses, some that look like they were ordered straight from a catalog. They weren't big, but they did the job. I’m running for re-election because there is still more work to do, and I would be honored to continue serving the people of the 14th Assembly District.
candidates.leg_q2: The top issue facing families in the 14th Assembly District is the rising cost of living. Too many people are struggling to afford housing, child care, utilities, health care, groceries, and other everyday necessities. I believe we need to make Wisconsin more affordable for working families by expanding access to affordable housing, lowering prescription drug costs, investing in child care, and supporting good-paying union jobs that help people keep up with rising expenses. We must also strengthen public education and workforce development programs so residents can access economic opportunities and build financial security. My focus is on practical solutions that help families get ahead and ensure everyone has the opportunity to thrive.
candidates.leg_q3: Wisconsin government should be more transparent, accountable, and responsive to the people it serves. For too long, partisan gridlock and political division have prevented progress on issues that matter to working families. Government works best when elected officials listen to their constituents, engage respectfully with those who hold different views, and focus on solving problems rather than scoring political points. I believe we need a government that is accessible, ethical, and committed to serving the public interest. That means increasing transparency in decision-making, investing in public services, and ensuring every Wisconsinite has a voice in our democracy. By working collaboratively and putting people first, we can build a stronger Wisconsin for everyone.
candidates.leg_q4: One of my favorite Wisconsin history facts is our state’s long tradition of progressivism, conservation, and support for working people. Wisconsin was the first state in the nation to enact workers’ compensation in 1911, helping protect workers and their families. Wisconsin also played a key role in the environmental movement. Earth Day was founded by former Governor and U.S. Senator Gaylord Nelson, inspiring millions of people worldwide to take action to protect our planet. These traditions reflect some of Wisconsin’s best values, where we look out for one another, protect our natural resources, and use government as a force for good. I’m proud to carry forward that Wisconsin legacy!

candidates.name: Stephen Tryon
candidates.occupation: Federal Express global dangerous goods specialist
candidates.leg_q1: Voters in Assembly District 15 deserve an independent-minded leader who answers strictly to the community, not to national party bosses. My life demonstrates commitment to service and real-world problem-solving. As a retired Army lieutenant colonel, I spent over two decades protecting our Constitution and leading soldiers. Later, as a business executive, I mastered how to build future-ready, technologically transparent systems. Most recently, my hands-on work as a courier and dangerous goods specialist in parcel delivery has kept me grounded in our day-to-day economy and deeply connected to the practical safety and infrastructure needs of working families. I have seen every corner of our district in good weather and bad. The model I describe in my book Accountability Citizenship will improve your state government.
candidates.leg_q2: The top issue facing Assembly District 15 is modernizing our infrastructure. Safe drinking water, future-ready public transit, and a resilient grid are the building blocks of local affordability and quality of life. Currently, our community remains vulnerable;  I have spoken with residents who routinely lose power for days due to vulnerable above-ground lines, others who are concerned about the health risks posed by PFAS and other substances in our drinking water. Our roads, sewage, internet, and school facilities must be better equipped for extreme weather. Wisconsin must stop letting career politicians use the budget surplus for short-term payouts. I will move our district from a reactive crisis-management model to a proactive strategy that secures our grid, protects our resources, and anticipates future growth.
candidates.leg_q3: Wisconsin state government must transition away from partisan gridlock and return to a service-first model focused on building and maintaining safe, informed and engaged communities. This is the essence of the information-age citizenship I described in my first book, Accountability Citizenship — the model I want to implement as your Assemblyman. Our state's immediate priorities should be public safety, modern (weather-proof) infrastructure, and high-quality education. Because federal dysfunction directly threatens Wisconsin's economic stability, our state legislature should proactively exercise its authority under Article V of the U.S. Constitution to lead the charge for critical federal reforms, including congressional term limits, a balanced-budget amendment, and meaningful campaign finance reform. We must stop allowing career politicians to divide our communities.
candidates.leg_q4: Arthur MacArthur Sr. was a Scottish immigrant who, while serving as lieutenant governor, was made the fourth governor of Wisconsin for only four days in March 1856 due to a dispute over the result of the 1855 gubernatorial election. Arthur MacArthur Sr. was the father of Arthur MacArthur (Civil War hero) and the grandfather of Douglas MacArthur.

candidates.name: Kalan Haywood
candidates.leg_q1: I was first elected to the Assembly at 19, and now in my fourth term I have learned how to show up for this community and deliver real results. I helped pass the shared revenue deal that brought property tax relief to Milwaukee families, protected thousands of local jobs, and expanded affordable housing across our city. As Assistant Minority Leader, I work across the aisle when it serves my constituents and stand firm when it counts. I do not just talk about change. I have a record of getting it done. I am running again because the work is not finished, and I want to keep fighting for the families, students, and workers who call the 16th District home.
candidates.leg_q2: Housing. Too many families in the 16th District are priced out of safe, stable homes, and rising costs are pushing longtime neighbors out of the neighborhoods they helped build. I have already fought to expand affordable housing, and there is more to do. We need to invest in new and rehabilitated units, support first-time homebuyers and renters, hold negligent landlords accountable, and protect families from displacement. Stable housing is the foundation for everything else, including good schools, safe streets, and strong local businesses. I will keep pushing for state investment that meets the scale of the need so that working families can afford to live, raise their kids, and build a future right here in Milwaukee.
candidates.leg_q3: For too long, Madison has put partisan games ahead of people. That has to change. With fair maps finally in place, voters have a real voice again, and government should reflect that by actually listening to the communities it serves. We proved progress is possible when the shared revenue deal passed with both parties at the table and delivered for cities like Milwaukee. I want more of that. Government should invest in people rather than score points, measure success by results in our neighborhoods, and be transparent about how it spends taxpayer dollars. When we focus on schools, jobs, housing, and safety instead of ideology, we get a Wisconsin that works for everyone, not just the well connected.
candidates.leg_q4: In 1854, right here in Milwaukee, a community stood up for what was right. Joshua Glover, a man who had escaped slavery and built a life near Racine, was captured under the Fugitive Slave Act and locked in the Milwaukee jail. Word spread fast, and thousands of people marched downtown, broke down the jailhouse door, and freed him. He reached freedom in Canada along the Underground Railroad. The outrage ran so deep that Wisconsin became the only state in the nation whose Supreme Court declared that federal slave-catching law unconstitutional. I love this story because it shows who we have always been: a community that refuses to look away from injustice and keeps pushing things Forward.

candidates.leg_q1: I am dedicated to serving my neighbors and community by representing their interests. I believe that the state of Wisconsin should do a better job of moving resources to local schools and neighborhoods. I am a collaborative leader who listens to my constituents and works with community to find solutions.
candidates.leg_q2: Affordability is the top issue across my district. It takes shape in different ways — an expanding food desert in one part of the district intensifies food insecurity. In another part of the district, senior citizens can no longer afford property taxes and are forced to leave their neighborhoods. Everywhere prices for gas, groceries, and rent are high. candidates.leg_q3: Wisconsin should re-invest in public education and support unionized labor. It should roll back unfair and unproductive restrictions on Milwaukee to address issues of tenant safety.

We have a strong dedication to the democratic principles of freedom and people-centered public policy. I hope we recapture our status as the state that leads the way in public health, public transportation, educational excellence and environmental protection.

candidates.name: Ryan Clancy
candidates.elected_experience: Wisconsin State Assembly (2023-present); Milwaukee Country Board (2020-2023)
candidates.leg_q1: I’ve spent my life listening to and fighting for Milwaukee. The policy that I write and pass is grounded in the thousands of conversations I’ve had with people all around the district for many years. From the right to counsel, which provides legal assistance to families facing eviction, to paid parental leave, to pushing back on the most harmful Republican attacks on the working class, immigrants, trans folks and Palestinians, my legislation and advocacy has had a positive impact on our district and the state. I show up, I listen, and I advocate for our city and residents.
candidates.leg_q2: The Trump regime’s overreach and attacks on our residents continues to be the issue that many residents are the most concerned about. From the threat of ICE being deployed in full force to Milwaukee, to attacks on essential services and benefits like Foodshare and Medicaid, and to the wars and tariffs which are making so many essentials unaffordable, it falls on the state to put policies and funding in place to push back on Trump’s attacks and to protect our residents. I’ve led on those efforts at the state, organizing my colleagues around scores of pieces of legislation; we’re eager to win the governor’s seat, the Senate and the Assembly in November so that we can finally get this legislation passed into law.
candidates.leg_q3: In November, when we have the trifecta, Democrats must lead boldly. The last trifecta (2009-10) we failed to deliver on popular policies like raising the minimum wage and codifying abortion rights. Democrats then lost control of the legislature for more than a decade and a half. This time, we have to do better. That means electing and supporting people who will fight for our community rather than compromising their values to try to appease the far right. It means both repealing Act 10 and providing the local revenue to pay workers fairly. It means codifying our rights and protections. It means fairly funding public education. And it means lowering property taxes by more than 40%  by having the extremely wealthy finally pay their fair share.
candidates.leg_q4: Wisconsin has elected socialists to nearly every level of government: school board directors, county board supervisors, city council members, mayors, even members of Congress. We had a lull for a while, though: when I was elected in 2020, I was the first since 1956. But when Wisconsin elects a democratic socialist as governor in November, she’ll be the first democratic socialist governor not only in Wisconsin’s history, but the first in the United States!

candidates.leg_q2: Unfortunately, this district has been underserved for many decades. The list of issues is long. My policies will address the most urgent needs of my constituents and neighbors.
candidates.leg_q3: By holding politicians accountable. Do not put your trust into someone who makes false promises and refuse to answer your phone calls after you got him/her into office. Vote Outlaw!

candidates.name: Bridget Maniaci
candidates.leg_q1: "With deep roots in Milwaukee and four years of elected experience as a progressive alderperson, I have a clear focus on delivering funds and state resources to help District 19 and Milwaukee. The incumbent has failed to get any legislation votes in four years AND hasn’t leveraged state resources. Frequently crusading for international and federal causes, he’s consistently voted against critical state spending for Milwaukee (Act 12) and chooses protests over results without focus on the role and responsibilities of this position. He was out of the country for three weeks and silent when we experienced record flooding. I’ll use my office to be present in the community, lead the fight to improve infrastructure and funding, create more affordable housing, and make Milwaukee more accessible. "
candidates.leg_q2: Affordability is the resounding theme — including utility bills, groceries, and rent. Housing assessments and property taxes have been rising significantly, as are the cost of repairs to vehicles getting damaged navigating Milwaukee’s crumbling and flooding streets — issues driven by how Republicans systemically cut funds and governing resources from Milwaukee. The solution is changing state formulas for shared revenue to municipalities; investing in repealing commercial and manufacturing tax loopholes (billions of dollars) for infrastructure costs; funding climate resilient infrastructure, replacing lead pipes, and safe streets/pothole repairs. Lowering utility and grocery costs require muscular regulatory oversight against monopolistic and peak pricing behavior. Lowering rents can happen through expanded WHEDA funds and incentive programs, reinstating and expanding pre-2011 tenant protection laws, and annual caps on rent increases.
candidates.leg_q3: The biggest change we need is how Wisconsin’s government has long undermined Milwaukee both legislatively and fiscally. Our schools, taxes, roads: This city is Wisconsin’s economic engine, and we need the state to invest in our infrastructure, quality, and affordability. The state surplus shows there is money available, but we’re not being set up for success. I have a roadmap for how to open up hidden fund opportunities that Milwaukee can leverage for use in new housing, park infrastructure, better transit, and safer streets for everyone. As climate change drives more interest in relocations to Milwaukee, I’m prepared and experienced in utilizing public funding and revenue sources to build Milwaukee for its future and move beyond the trauma of its past disinvestment.
candidates.leg_q4: I love that Dungeons & Dragons was created in Wisconsin, and that the manuscripts for The Lord of the Rings trilogy permanently reside here. With all of its beer, Wisconsinites may be seen as happy Hobbits in the Shire, but a real Trumpian Eye of Mordor regularly turns its attention here and we need to ready a collaborative defense of our precious democracy. During the pandemic, I built new friendships playing D&D. Using imagination and storytelling abilities to fight trolls across faraway lands is a helpful real life skill set today. D&D is great training for working with colleagues to accomplish the incredible. As your state representative, I will use similar teamwork to find smart, creative solutions to our problems in real life.

candidates.name: David Liners
candidates.leg_q1: Mine will be a clear voice for progressive change and economic fairness in Madison. Being an Assembly representative will be my fulltime job. I am a lifelong advocate for social justice, not a career politician. I will listen to constituents and will be transparent, even when I know people do not agree with me.
candidates.leg_q2: People are very worried about the future of public schools. And, they are concerned about property taxes. We need to restructure the way we pay for schools (and childcare, and health care) by raising corporate and upper-income tax rates so the state can pick up a greater share of the total costs. The second biggest concern is data centers; we need a moratorium on construction while we sort it out.
candidates.leg_q3: Wisconsin's government, especially the legislature, needs to be much more transparent. We need an end to deals made in back rooms that result in things like the $1.5 billion tax break for data center construction. We need to be open about the tradeoffs when policy is made, and we need legislators and the governor to be held accountable for their decisions. We need public hearings with adequate notice, and not just rushed hearings called after leadership has already made its decision.
candidates.leg_q4: Wisconsin is the birthplace of so many good things:  Workers' comp; primary elections; rural free mail delivery, the first kindergarten (in my hometown!), Earth Day and the electric guitar, to name a few. Though we occasionally come up with a stinker, like Joe McCarthy, we have been leaders in the U.S., and we can be again.

candidates.name: Daniel J. Bukiewicz

candidates.leg_q1: I didn't start in a boardroom. I started on a jobsite as an apprentice electrician in Milwaukee. I have spent my career fighting for working families at the bargaining table and in public office, and I know what it means to live the struggles our neighbors face every day. As mayor of Oak Creek I have delivered real results for businesses and families for 18 years. I am the only candidate in this race with local government experience, and the only one who has truly lived the working class story of the voters I am asking to represent. I will be a champion for working families in Madison, not a rubber stamp for special interests.
candidates.leg_q2: The cost of living is crushing working families in the 21st Assembly District. Groceries, rent, healthcare and everyday expenses keep rising while paychecks struggle to keep up. I will fight to raise Wisconsin's minimum wage to $20 an hour, expand BadgerCare and create a public option so no one has to choose between rent and a doctor. I will also fight to fully fund our public schools so local communities are not forced to make up the difference through property tax increases. When the state meets its obligation to fund education, families and homeowners win. These are common sense solutions that put working families first.
candidates.leg_q3: Wisconsin government needs to stop working for corporations and special interests and start working for the people who built this state. For too long, working families have been ignored while those at the top write the rules. That has to change. Government should be a tool for lifting people up, not holding them down. That means fully funding our public schools, expanding access to affordable healthcare, raising wages and investing in the communities that need it most. I have spent my entire career as a servant leader, fighting for working families at the bargaining table and in city hall. That is exactly the kind of leadership I will bring to Madison.
candidates.leg_q4: My favorite Wisconsin history fact is one most people don't know: Milwaukee is the birthplace of the typewriter. The first commercially successful typewriter was produced right here in 1873. Milwaukee has always been a city of workers, builders, innovators, and others who make things with their hands. That spirit is alive and well today, and it is exactly what I am fighting to preserve as your representative in Madison.

candidates.leg_q1: I am a 26-year Ozaukee County resident, educator, and military wife and mother. I’m committed to representing every resident of this district and addressing the concerns I hear from my neighbors; from the rising cost of living, to the strain on public education funding and its impact on property taxes, to the protection of our land and natural resources. I will bring this experience and passion to Madison to advocate for the families of our district.
candidates.leg_q2: Families in Assembly District 22 are feeling the squeeze of rising costs. From housing and property taxes to childcare and healthcare, affordability has become the biggest challenge shaping daily life in our communities. Our district attracts many new families and residents want to stay here, raise their families here, and retire here. But it is getting harder and too many are struggling to keep up. I will reach across the aisle to address these issues. We must end the vicious cycle of underfunding our public schools, community referenda and property tax increases, and I will work to expand access to affordable healthcare and childcare.  Addressing affordability is key to keeping our district strong, vibrant, and a place where every family can thrive.
candidates.leg_q3: For too long, Wisconsin’s state government has been hamstrung by partisan gridlock and a lack of transparency maintained by the Republican majority. With fairer legislative maps now in place, we finally have an opportunity to restore bipartisan cooperation and ensure that every community’s voice is heard in Madison.

Responsible spending and accountable government help ensure communities can continue providing the services people rely on while maintaining the quality of life our district expects. Giving Wisconsinites the opportunity to keep more of their hard-earned money through tax relief is another important part of improving affordability and helping families manage rising everyday costs.
candidates.leg_q3: The Wisconsin government needs to spend smarter and legislate more effectively. Taxpayers deserve greater transparency, stronger oversight, and regular audits to ensure public funds are being used efficiently and delivering measurable results.

candidates.name: Deb Andraca
candidates.leg_q1: When I was elected in 2020 I promised to fight for a safer, smarter, healthier Wisconsin. Since day one I have done my best to represent all my constituents, whether they voted for me or not. I hold weekly in-district office hours and bring constituents' voices to all my work in Madison. As a member of the Joint Finance Committee I supported increasing state funding for K-12 education to help hold the line on property taxes, lowering everyday costs including child care and higher education, investing in conservation programs, and funding for safe communities and violence prevention. I will continue this important work if the voters elect me to serve another term.
candidates.leg_q2: Families are being squeezed by rising costs, in particular groceries, child care, higher education and housing. First we must ensure we are keeping taxes low for families in the middle and lower income brackets to help them afford everyday needs. The state must live up to its commitment to fully fund public schools to relieve pressure on property taxes and invest in the UW System. To make child care more affordable and accessible, we must help certified child care providers open more classrooms and recruit and retain qualified staff. Finally, in partnership with local municipalities, we need to encourage the development of more housing units to drive down the cost of rent and home ownership.
candidates.leg_q3: Our government should serve the people, not a political party, which means more public hearings, open exchange of ideas, listening to constituents, and working across the aisle to create the best outcomes for Wisconsin. When I was elected my district was 50% Republican and 50% Democratic, which also reflects the state as a whole. I understand how important it is to have an open mind and to listen to all points of view. Wisconsin used to be a national model for bipartisanship and clean, open government and we must find a way to restore our legacy of democratic (small D) reforms.

candidates.name: Joe Sheehan
candidates.leg_q1: For over 20 years, I served as superintendent of the Sheboygan Area School District. During that time, I learned the value of collaboration. Over the past two years it has been an honor to serve as the 26th Assembly District’s representative, and I brought that experience with me. Above all I listen to the input of the people around me, and when serving my constituents I try to listen as much as I can. My process for solving problems has always been to bring experts and those affected to the table and then forming a solution collaboratively.
candidates.leg_q2: As I have been out knocking on doors, I continuously hear about the issues caused by the rising cost of living. Progress can only come from open conversation. Here in Wisconsin, we need to make sure we are at least giving both sides a chance to discuss their ideas and get input from the public.
candidates.leg_q4: Bob Lafollette being the only third-party candidate to receive electoral college votes for the presidency, receiving Wisconsin’s votes in the 1924 election. The roots of progressive politics are strong in Wisconsin, and Lafollette is a great example of that.

candidates.name: Tyler Schneekloth

I seek to reduce our state income tax, offer interest free home loans for young families and first time home buyers, and one of the only candidates in the 26th Assembly District in favor of a temporary moratorium on ai data centers. Expanding WHEDA and offering interest free mortgages to young families and first time home owners will encourage new homes being built and pull younger people away from expensive unaffordable apartments, which should in turn reduce rent prices as well as allowing younger generations to plant their roots and stay in our local communities.
candidates.leg_q3: We should be paying down our state debt of $54 billion with any and all surpluses until our debt is below $10 billion. This debt is a future tax on younger generations, and by being responsible now, we can reduce our overall taxes in the future.

candidates.name: Kevin Knoke
candidates.leg_q1: One of the best parts of being a teacher was knowing that every day I had the chance to make someone's life a little better. I'm running for the Wisconsin Assembly because I want to continue serving others and making a difference. I want to go to Madison and do what I did in the classroom: listen, solve problems, and help people. As your representative, I'll be a tenacious advocate for working families, farmers, seniors and small businesses of the 30th Assembly District. My goal is simple: work hard, fight for western Wisconsin, and make life a little better for the people I serve.
candidates.leg_q2: The rising cost of living, especially healthcare costs, is a major concern for families across the 30th Assembly District. It's critical that we expand access to affordable health insurance for working families so no family is one medical emergency away from bankruptcy. We also need to lower prescription drug prices, improve access to mental health services, and increase access to quality care across the state. By increasing transparency and competition in the healthcare marketplace, we can make quality care more affordable and accessible for everyone. If we fail to act, more Wisconsinites will be forced to go without health insurance or delay the care they need, putting their health and financial security at risk. Wisconsin families deserve better.
candidates.leg_q3: The Legislature must start putting working families first. We need to address the rising costs and growing challenges facing our communities by expanding access to affordable healthcare, quality childcare, and reliable services for seniors. We must also reaffirm our commitment to public education from our K-12 schools to our technical colleges, trade programs, and universities, because a strong education system is the foundation of a strong economy.
candidates.leg_q4: I was a public school teacher for 26 years.  Most of those years, I taught fifth grade. My favorite part of our academic day was social studies.  It was during this time that I got to share my love of history. I’ve always loved American history, especially the story of the Civil War. During the Civil War, nearly 1 in 9 Wisconsinites served in the Union Army. More than 91,000 citizens answered the call to preserve the Union, including over half of all eligible Wisconsin voters at the time. Their courage, sacrifice, and commitment to our nation helped shape the Wisconsin we know today. It's a remarkable legacy, one worth remembering, and it makes me proud to be a Wisconsinite.

candidates.name: John Perryman
candidates.leg_q1: My 33-year career in medicine has given me a unique insight into the struggles so many of us face: affordability, getting the health care we need, getting a good education for our kids, and keeping families safe. My opponent, Republican Tyler August and I have very different views on many issues. I will fight to expand health care, he restricts it. I will work to make sure our public schools are well funded, he has restricted funding. I will fight to raise the minimum wage and strengthen unions, he would weaken them. The list goes on. I will bring change to our state government and work to represent everyone in our district, not just wealthy donors.
candidates.leg_q2: Affordability and high property taxes. One of the big drivers for high costs are medical expenses. At the state level, this can be addressed by price caps on common medicines, limiting the amount of out-of-pocket costs incurred by patients, and working to reduce administrative costs, among others, The root cause of high property tax is inadequate state funding of our public schools, which leads communities to rely on repeated property tax hikes. candidates.leg_q3: We need to focus on making government work for everyone, not just the wealthy. There needs to be a focus on the economic stressors families face (housing, child care, health care, utilities, etc) and an effort to bring government policy to bear on fixing these problems. We also need to take a longer-term approach to fundamental challenges we face, such as AI and climate change.

candidates.name: Greg Miller
candidates.leg_q1: As representative, I'll listen to all residents. My opponent often ignores the needs of voters in the 32nd District, in favor of the special interests that fund her. Representatives must work for the good of all, not just the wealthy. I will work to ensure that the benefits of government are shared fairly. After years of one-party rule, new approaches are needed. Average taxpayers spend billions, yet rarely see the benefits. Cuts to healthcare and education must be restored and property tax burdens reduced. I am a young candidate, bringing new energy. My background as an Eagle Scout and five years in the Air Force taught me to act with integrity, with a spirit of service. No one will worker harder for the 32nd District.
candidates.leg_q2: The top issue in District 32 is the over-reliance on property tax. This affects many government services and is most harmful to public school funding. Under the last sixteen years of one-party rule the legislature has negligently allowed school funding to lag, harming children’s educations and putting extreme fiscal pressure on homeowners, small businesses and school boards. My proposal is to remove private school funding from property tax rolls. Vouchers should be funded from general revenue, if at all. Public schools would be allowed to keep current funding when private schools are removed, closing funding gaps. This would ensure that progressive income tax rates fund private benefits, not regressive property taxes. Furthermore, public and private schools should be funded equally in all areas.
candidates.leg_q3: Power in the Legislature is too concentrated. The speaker’s control over the legislative agenda and committee appointments stifles legislation that the majority of Wisconsinites support, causing public frustration and undermining people’s faith in government. There needs to be mechanisms in place to allow bills with sufficient support to move efficiently and increase public participation. One way to do that is to allow more public hearings on bills. Not only does this reduce the ability of the speaker to manipulate the agenda, hearings allow the public a greater opportunity to see the legislative process and to participate in it. Wisconsin was historically one of the first states to champion open government and must be so again.
candidates.leg_q4: I take pride that during the Civil War, the Wisconsin second, sixth, and eight regiments made up a majority of the highly coveted Iron Brigade. This brigade defended against Stonewall Jackson at the second battle of Bull Run, and stood its ground at the battles of Antietam and Gettysburg. Later in the war the Iron Brigade took part in the Overland Campaign and the siege of Petersburg that destroyed Robert Lee's Army of the Potomac.

candidates.name: Rick Stacey
candidates.elected_experience: Walworth County Board  (2004-2015, 2018-present); board chair (4 years)
candidates.leg_q1: Wisconsin's future depends on responsible government spending. Our state is currently BROKE — budget and bureaucracy. It's bogged down by red tape, managed by out of touch oversight and it is denying our families opportunity through excessive spending. We need common sense leadership that puts our hard-working communities back in the driver's seat. I will fight for our families on the state level just as I've done in my county.
candidates.leg_q2: Taxes, affordability and housing. High taxes and restrictive mandates are draining resources from local families, hindering regional growth and stalling critical infrastructure repairs. Madison relies on a top-down, one size fits all approach that suffocates small business, multigenerational farms and local economies. I plan to fight for local communities by eliminating the red tape and bureaucracy.
candidates.leg_q3: It's time for less government and fewer regulations. It is time to put money back in our pockets and make living affordable.
candidates.leg_q4: It's incredible all the businesses and innovations that were born and continue to grow in our great state — Case IH, Mercury Marine, Kohler, Usinger, Harley Davidson, Northwestern Mutual — this list goes on and on. All while maintaining the title America's Dairyland.

candidates.name: Steve Wicklund
candidates.leg_q1: Voters should elect me because I've done the job at the level closest to the people. As village president of Union Grove, I've delivered fiscal discipline, responsible growth, and accountable government. As chair of the Racine County Intergovernmental Cooperation Council, I work with local leaders to strengthen partnerships and protect local decision-making. As a small business owner, I've seen firsthand how excessive regulation, rising costs, and government overreach burden working families and employers. I'm not running to start a political career; I'm running to bring proven local leadership to Madison. Madison should work for the people, not control them. I believe in the people of Racine and Walworth counties, and I'm ready to fight for the values that built this district.
candidates.leg_q2: The top issue in our district is affordability, and property taxes are where families feel it most. Madison increased school revenue limits while holding state aid flat, pushing costs onto local property taxpayers, and homeowners saw it in their December tax bills on top of rising grocery, energy, and housing costs. As village president of Union Grove, I've balanced budgets by setting priorities, not by reaching deeper into taxpayers' pockets, and I'll bring that same discipline to Madison. I'll work to reduce the property tax burden, return state surpluses to the people who paid them, restore the balance between state aid and local levies, and oppose mandates that drive up local costs. Families shouldn't be taxed out of the communities they built.
candidates.leg_q3: Wisconsin government should operate closer to the people it serves. Too many decisions get made in Madison and handed down to communities as unfunded mandates and one-size-fits-all rules. As chair of the Racine County Intergovernmental Cooperation Council, I've seen what's possible when state and local governments work as partners instead of adversaries, and that's the model I'll bring to the Assembly. That means respecting local decision-making, funding the responsibilities the state assigns, budgeting with the same discipline families and small businesses use, and returning surpluses to taxpayers rather than growing government. It also means accessibility: legislators should spend more time at kitchen tables and village halls than in Capitol hallways. Madison should work for the people, not control them.
candidates.leg_q4: Growing up, I heard the older generation talk about "oleo runs," and I thought they were pulling my leg. They weren't. Until 1967, selling yellow margarine was banned in Wisconsin, so families would drive across the Illinois border and come home with trunks full of it, like butter-colored moonshine. Grandmothers who never broke a rule in their lives were smuggling margarine past the state line. That's how seriously we take dairy here. And my favorite part: to this day, a Wisconsin restaurant can't serve you margarine instead of butter unless you ask for it. Some laws protect people. This one protects butter. Having spent my life around hardworking Wisconsin families, I understand it completely. The cows earned it, and so did we.

candidates.name: Maria Elena Bisabarros
candidates.leg_q1: I want to bring money from the state to my district schools, farmers, fire departments, small businesses and roads. The local communities are not getting enough money to survive but the state is giving $1.5 billion from the public money in sales tax credit for construction marerials and equipment to the data centers being built in Wisconsin.
candidates.leg_q2: Public education. Our school districts cannot balance their budget because they are losing millions of dollars every year due to the vouchers going to private schools and open enrollment going to out of the district schools.
candidates.leg_q3: We need to support our small local communities instead of the big corporations and put a moratorium on data centers until we, the residents, decide and vote if we want a data center in our town due to the use of our water and energy. AI should be used in research and to reduce work that benefits human beings, not to diminish our human abilities and take away our privacy.
candidates.leg_q4: The first kindergarten in the U.S. was established in Watertown in 1856.

candidates.name: Rick Bailey
candidates.leg_q1: I decided that I could no longer watch the chaos in D.C. and the gridlock in Madison. I am running to represent the hard working people in District 33: families, small business owners, farmers, people who need government assistance (Medicare, Medicaid, affordable access to health care, regulation of AI plus open Information and local public control of building AI plants, our precious environment.). Time to listen to the people not the wealthiest. I also hope to make our tax codes fairer, that the top tier pay their fair share. I also believe that we must fund all of our public schools equally and in a manner where they don’t have to conduct yearly or bi-yearly referendums just to maintain services for kids.
candidates.leg_q2: Affordability is the most pressing issue for most Wisconsin families. Due to the actions of the current administration in Washington, and the almost complete rubber stamping of their policies by the Republican majorities there along with the gridlock between the Republican controlled legislature and our governor, middle class and working people are finding it harder to keep up with the cost of living:  groceries, gas prices, hime cooling and heating bills. Tariffs enacted by Washington have begun to cause inflation to rise, raising the cost of everyday necessities for many, as well as the cutting of funding to states for infrastructure and relief. I would emphatically propose and support any legislative initiative that brings some much needed financial relief to the people of District 33.
candidates.leg_q3: For far too long now politicians must pass “purity” tests not only to win elections but to maintain the needed financial support from powerful lobbies and big donors or risk defeat. Money has way too much control over not only Wisconsin but the entire country. If we are to again function with any hope of efficiency, any hope to return to the art of discussion, debate, truly listening, compromise, as our founding fathers believed we must to a great degree eliminate the  clout the wealthiest have over our political system. U.S. Supreme Court decisions since the late 1970s, most notably Citizens United, are tearing us apart.
candidates.leg_q4: As a former high school social studies teacher I would have to say is the legacy of progressivism and the career of leaders such as Fighting Bob LaFollette.  During his entire career, first as a U.S. congressman from 1885 to 1891, then governor of our state from 1901 to 1906, then his 20-year career as U.S. Senator, LaFollette was always a strong advocate for the working people of Wisconsin. I have always admired his ability to grow as a politician during his long career, first as a Republican then as a leading voice of the Progressive Party that he created in 1924. We need his far sighted, human-based thinking now more than ever.

candidates.leg_q1: Voters deserve respectful representation — a representative who shows up in and for the community. I am that respectful representative — with a track record of working for the people in local government and in community organizations. I've done real work and there is just no substitute for real work.
candidates.leg_q2: It’d be nice if there was one "top" issue — but housing, (the tip of the issue iceberg) is tied to child care and elder services, and child care is just step 1 of Education. Together they make up a noose that strangles communities. The step that can cut the noose is variety. We need a variety of housing, not just many identical units mass produced but unsuitable for the neediest home seekers. We need those housing options clustered around different amenities depending upon the needs of different sectors of our community and we need multiple price and size points because one size does not fit all and it makes the problem worse. My strategy focuses on housing variety keyed to amenities and service areas.
candidates.leg_q3: The single most important thing that must change in Wisconsin is how electoral maps are created. Gerrymandering is bad for all parties — even the party that engineers it — because it isolates lawmakers from electoral consequences. Voters are effectively disenfranchised and election winners have no accountability and act with reckless impunity. Wisconsin cannot afford to have lawmakers who do not actually answer to the people.
candidates.leg_q4: My favorite fact is that Wisconsin was the undisputed leader in circuses in the 19th century, birthing over 100 travelling shows. candidates.name: Shena Chapman
candidates.leg_q1: It’s time for a change in the 36th District. Our communities face real challenges. PFAS contamination impacts families, and schools struggle with funding. These issues cannot be ignored, and I’m ready to fight for the solutions our district deserves. I’m running for Assembly as an independent because I believe people should come before politics. Party agendas aren't my priority — our community is. My focus will always be on what is best for the people of the 36th District. I’ll listen to the voices of our residents, work across political lines, and fight for practical solutions that strengthen our communities, support our schools, and protect our future. If you are ready for a representative who puts our community first, I would be honored to earn your vote.
candidates.leg_q2: The top issue facing our district is PFAS contamination. Clean, safe water is essential, and many families in our communities are concerned about the long-term impact PFAS may have on their health and quality of life. I will address this issue by working closely with residents, scientists, environmental experts, local leaders, and state agencies to fully understand the challenges we face and identify the most effective solutions. I will advocate for available funding to be used efficiently and fight for additional resources to support cleanup efforts and protect our communities. Just as importantly, I will ensure transparency throughout the process so residents have access to accurate information and understand the progress being made.
candidates.leg_q3: Wisconsin government should operate differently by putting people before politics. Too often, partisan divisions prevent progress on the issues that matter most to our communities. I believe elected officials should spend more time listening to the people they represent and less time focusing on political agendas. Government should be transparent, accountable, and focused on solving real problems. As an Independent candidate, my priority is not a political party — it is the people of the 36th District. When we focus on what is best for our communities and work together toward common goals, Wisconsin will be stronger for everyone.
candidates.leg_q4: One of my favorite Wisconsin history facts is that after the devastating Peshtigo Fire of 1871 — the deadliest wildfire in U.S. history — the people of the area rebuilt their communities despite unimaginable loss and hardship. What I appreciate most about this story is the resilience it represents. Wisconsin’s history is filled with people who faced challenges head-on, worked together, and refused to give up. That same spirit still exists in our communities today. The story of Peshtigo reminds us that even in difficult times, strong communities can recover, rebuild, and emerge stronger when people support one another and work toward a common goal.

candidates.leg_q1: I am a working mom, fighting for the change we need in Wisconsin. We have had nearly 14 years of the same party politics and finger pointing. It is time to get to work for Wisconsin and make sure everyone who is working hard and doing their best can stay and succeed here.
candidates.leg_q2: People cannot afford their basic needs. We need higher wages, better jobs, lower property taxes and support of small businesses and  farms.

candidates.name: Terri Wenkman
candidates.leg_q1: I'm a common sense leader who will listen and see the big picture! I refuse to get lost in social warfare when quality of life and affordability are at stake. I've lived in Jefferson my whole life and raised my family here. I'm a nurse of 20 years, serving people across many aspects of health care. I've served on our public school board since 2014 and have been engaged in education funding policy for over a decade. I've navigated the health care system, both for loved ones and as an advocate for persons with varying disabilities. I’m a fierce advocate, but also a deeply compassionate person. I believe we can legislate policies that work for everyone and not just those with money and lobbyists.
candidates.leg_q2: Affordable health care. People are making impossible choices and gambling with their health. Some skipping insurance coverage or delaying care because they simply can't afford it. Yet, rural hospitals depend on an insured population to stay open and attract quality doctors and nurses. That's a cycle that ends up hurting everyone. I've seen this as a nurse and as someone who navigated the system for loved ones. We need to expand access, reduce premium costs, and treat mental health as importantly as physical health. Mental health is health care. Rural communities are consistently left behind. I will fight for solutions that keep our hospitals viable, make coverage affordable, and ensure that where you live and income don't determine the quality of care you receive.
candidates.leg_q3: Wisconsin government must stop making working and middle class families absorb the cost of policies that benefit the few. Property taxpayers cannot sustain a system that funds both public schools and a parallel voucher system that drains resources without accountability. That's not fiscally conservative and not sustainable. We need to honestly examine the growing concentration of wealth and its impact on everyday Wisconsinites. When working families are being priced out of the communities they built, something is broken. Going forward, Wisconsin must change and expand health care subsidies, fix our school funding formula, and make decisions that stabilize the cost of living for working families.
candidates.leg_q4: Many people don't know that Rosemary Kennedy, sister of President John F. Kennedy, spent most of her life right here in Jefferson, Wisconsin. She lived at St. Coletta's for over 60 years, where I had the privilege of working as a nurse in the early 2000s. She received wonderful care there, and it inspired her sister Eunice to found the Special Olympics. St. Coletta's became a national model for serving people with intellectual disabilities right here in rural Wisconsin. Compassion and advocacy in action and where my professional roots started.

candidates.name: William Penterman
candidates.occupation: Staff sergeant in the U.S. Army Reserve, substitute teacher, State representative, and licensed real estate salesperson
candidates.leg_q1: I love problem-solving and getting things done. This session, I introduced over 20 unique pieces of legislation. Ten of those bills passed the Wisconsin State Assembly, and five were signed into law by the governor. Some of my more notable bills that became law include exempting state income tax for members of the National Guard and Reserves (AB 913), improving school bus safety (SB 391 and SB 392), and enhancing retail theft penalties (AB 89). Some politicians talk a big game about the things they want to do, but never deliver. I get things done.
candidates.leg_q2: The top issue in my district is affordability. In the past six years, the price of nearly everything has gone up significantly. “Free” money from the federal government during the coronavirus pandemic flooded the economy, and prices of goods and services have skyrocketed since. While this is a federal issue, the state government should not take in more than it needs to. I want hardworking Wisconsinites to keep more of their hard-earned money, because they can do a better job spending it than the state government can. I want to make Wisconsin’s tax code simpler and more competitive with other states. Finally, I want to promote strong families in Wisconsin. The family unit is the best, most efficient, and most effective unit to solve problems.
candidates.leg_q3: Wisconsin state government should increase transparency and accountability to ensure taxpayer dollars are spent as effectively and efficiently as possible. Specifically, the state should implement a system for the timely release of public records and provide the public with easier access to information about how every taxpayer dollar is allocated. Similar to CCAP, Wisconsin could create a searchable online database that allows residents to see which individuals, businesses, or organizations receive state funds, how much they receive, and the purpose of each expenditure. This would promote greater public oversight and help build trust in government spending decisions.
candidates.leg_q4: I also serve on the Wisconsin Historical Society Board of Curators, and love promoting Wisconsin history! Wisconsin has a rich heritage and strong history. My favorite historical fact is that Wisconsin is home to the birthplace of the Republican Party, at the Little White Schoolhouse in Ripon. This new party’s ideals of ending slavery, promoting individual liberty, and securing economic opportunity without government oppression continue to live on through the policies and platforms of Republican candidates to this day.

candidates.elected_experience: Wisconsin State Assembly (2025-present); Dane County Board (2012-present); DeForest Village Board (1999-2003)

candidates.leg_q2: Not surprisingly, affordability is clearly the No. 1 issue people are raising with me. candidates.name: Brienne Brown
candidates.elected_experience: Wisconsin State Assembly (2025-present); Whitewater Common Council (2019-2025)
candidates.leg_q1: I’m running for re-election to Assembly to fight for freedom, opportunity, and a stronger future for Wisconsin families. I’m a principled fighter who works in a bipartisan manner to get things done and deliver real results for our communities. Too often, the system is rigged for special interests instead of working people. I fight for the freedom to make reproductive choices without government interference and for freedom from gun violence. I’m committed to investing in public schools, roads, childcare, and affordable healthcare while reducing taxes on the middle class. I support our family farms, veterans, retirees, and small businesses. I have a proven record of fighting for clean water, good union jobs, and strong public education so everyone can achieve their dreams without crushing debt.
candidates.leg_q2: Affordability. Constituents tell me they cannot afford gas, groceries, medications, or doctor visits. Parents struggle with high costs of childcare even as childcare centers close. Families are one accident, illness, or unexpected expense away from financial crisis. Others feel the strain of rising rents, mortgages, and property taxes as more costs shift onto local communities. We can address these challenges by expanding access to affordable healthcare and childcare, increasing the supply of workforce housing, reducing prescription drug costs, supporting family-sustaining wages, and providing meaningful property tax relief. We must invest in strong public schools and infrastructure that help families and businesses thrive. Wisconsin's economy is strongest when working families can afford to live, raise children, and build secure futures in the communities they call home.
candidates.leg_q3: For too long, Wisconsin's government has become more focused on winning political battles than solving problems. The legislative process works best when ideas are heard, debated, and improved through public input and open discussion. Unfortunately, committee hearings have too often been limited, and opportunities for bipartisan collaboration have been missed. Wisconsin government should operate with greater transparency, respect, and a commitment to finding common ground. Legislators should be encouraged to engage with differing viewpoints, listen to constituents, and evaluate proposals on their merits rather than their political origin. When debate is allowed and diverse perspectives are welcomed, better solutions emerge. Our responsibility is not to score political points, but to work together to deliver results that improve the lives of all Wisconsinites.
candidates.leg_q4: Wisconsin has long been a state of firsts, leading the nation in strengthening democracy and improving lives. We were the first state to ratify the 19th Amendment, helping secure women’s right to vote. We pioneered direct primary elections, opening the political process to voters instead of party machines. We led the nation in creating workers’ compensation and later became the first state to establish unemployment insurance. Wisconsin helped define the Wisconsin Idea through UW-Madison, proving that research and government can directly serve the public good. We were early leaders in cooperative movements that strengthened family farms and rural economies, and we helped lay the groundwork for public broadcasting and educational radio. It all started with innovation in education, like the nation’s first kindergarten in Watertown.
