candidates.leg_q2: The top issue in our district is the intertwined housing affordability and property tax crisis, which threatens young families, seniors, and rural communities.
candidates.leg_q3: Wisconsin government should operate with fiscal discipline, accountability, and a focus on results instead of endless spending and partisanship. I'll bring small-business principles to Madison: invest smartly for measurable returns, prioritize workforce readiness for the AI economy.
candidates.leg_q4: My favorite fun Wisconsin history fact is that the ice cream sundae was invented in Two Rivers, Wisconsin, in 1881. A local soda fountain owner served ice cream topped with chocolate syrup — something previously only used in sodas — after a customer requested it on a Sunday. The town still celebrates this sweet legacy today. As a small business owner myself, I love this story of Wisconsin innovation and entrepreneurship turning a simple request into an American classic.

candidates.name: Bill Oemichen
candidates.occupation: Full-time professor of practice, law/local government law educator, UW-Madison Division of Extension
candidates.elected_experience: New Glarus Board of Education (2018-present), board president (2020-present); St. Croix County Board (1989-1996)
candidates.leg_q1: I bring the experience and urgency needed to deliver results from day one. As a school board president, I’ve confronted Wisconsin’s broken state funding model and understand the path to fixing it. My family helped found Prairie Haus in New Glarus, a nationally recognized affordable community for disabled and typically abled tenants. I work directly with communities to expand affordable senior cooperative housing. I’ve been an agricultural and cooperative leader and co‑created a health care cooperative for Wisconsin farmers who lacked access to insurance. I served on the Monroe Clinic and Group Health Cooperative boards to strengthen high‑quality care in South Central Wisconsin. As volunteer Edvest board chair, I’ve championed early saving to reduce reliance on costly student loans since 2004.
candidates.leg_q2: The Republican Legislature has repeatedly failed to properly fund public schools while significantly expanding taxpayer support for private school vouchers. The 2025-27 state budget provides no increase in equalization aid funding and only a minimal boost for Special Education, forcing districts to repeatedly rely on property tax referendums just to keep up with inflation. Meanwhile, taking the private school voucher program statewide adds an estimated $1.8 billion to the state budget over the biennium. Strong public schools are the backbone of thriving communities. Wisconsin must renew its commitment to fully funding public education and return more of that responsibility to the income tax which reflects ability to pay. Relying on property taxes instead places an unfair burden on seniors and others on fixed incomes.
candidates.leg_q3: My views are shaped by years of service on the New Glarus School Board, my work teaching local government law at UW-Madison Extension, and my prior roles as Wisconsin’s chief consumer advocate and as preparedness and emergency health care director. But the most urgent reform is securing fair legislative maps. Partisan gerrymandering by the Republican Legislature since 2010 has distorted representation, creating uncompetitive districts where primaries — not general elections — decide outcomes. In effect, legislators chose their voters instead of voters choosing their representatives. Wisconsin must finally adopt a non‑partisan redistricting process conducted once every ten years. I will support legislative efforts to make this a reality. Our democracy must reflect the will of the people.
candidates.leg_q4: The Wisconsin Historical Society tells a story about two Oehmichen brothers from Manitowoc — my ancestors — who volunteered for the Union Army in the Civil War after arriving from 1848 Germany as part of the pro‑democracy migration. On their way from Manitowoc to Milwaukee to be mustered in, they reportedly convinced tavern owners that Union soldiers drank for free. This worked until Cedarburg where the tavern keeper demanded payment and the brothers expressed their disagreement by redecorating the furniture. Despite their creative accounting, they made it to Milwaukee, joined the Union Army, and served Wisconsin with honor. Their mix of mischief and commitment reminds me that courage, democracy, and a little humor often travel together.

candidates.name: Bryna Caves
candidates.leg_q1: As a nurse for the past 20 years, my adult life has been dedicated to caring for others. I spent most of my career working in intensive care units, giving me the skills necessary to be a calm, decisive leader in times of crises. I pride myself on being able to talk to anyone, but I really excel at speaking respectfully with people that don’t agree with me. Democracy is a team sport and I have the proven ability to work collaboratively and constructively with people of all backgrounds to achieve a goal, even in tense situations. Whether the goal is treating a cardiac event or passing legislation to protect us from data centers, I’ll be the clear leader that can get the job done.
candidates.leg_q2: Property taxes are number one concern I hear from my neighbors. From both Republicans and Democrats in my district, I am hearing the overall theme of things not being affordable anymore. The price of everything from gas to groceries to utility bills is continuing to go up, and wages are not. People are feeling squeezed, and looking for real relief. The first thing I would do to address this is fully fund our public schools and responsibly end the voucher system. If the schools have what they need, they won’t need to rely on this toxic cycle of property tax referendums. The state needs to use tax payer dollars to fund schools in the budget, fully, no exceptions.
candidates.leg_q3: We need to to get money out of politics. Hawaii just passed legislation to end Citizens United in their state and Wisconsin can do it too. We need to end politicians being able to trade individual stocks while sitting on committees that regulate the same industries they own. You cannot trust your officials to make decisions in the best interest of the people, if there are massive profits to be made if you vote a certain way. We also need to bring political civility back again. Love your neighbor.
candidates.leg_q4: Georgia O’Keeffe, one of my favorite artists, was born in Sun Prairie!

candidates.name: Ben Gruber
candidates.leg_q1: I’ve been serving my community for over 20 years; as an EMT, a firefighter, a police officer and conservation warden. I’ve been in homes across every corner of this district, and I see how hard people are working to make ends meet. I’ve seen that our elderly neighbors sometimes don’t have food in the fridge for tomorrow, and I’ve seen the teacher working the second shift at the gas station to pay for her daughter’s insulin. As a local leader, I know that it is time for new leadership that cares about working-class issues and will fight for our rural communities. I’ll fight to lower costs and stand up for our rural communities that have been left behind. I’ll stand up and fight for us.
candidates.leg_q2: We must fix public school funding. The GOP controlled-legislature has voted to take our money from public schools and funnel it to unaccountable private schools, leading to the closure of several of our rural public schools. As a result, we are constantly asked to raise our own property taxes just to keep the lights on at our local public school. We have to fulfill the state’s constitutional obligation to fund public schools and special education; and we must stop giving public money to private schools and end the cycle of property tax referendums to fund school operating costs.
candidates.leg_q3: Wisconsin government should operate differently by prioritizing our communities and working families, instead of the current prioritization of corporate welfare and pandering to the billionaire class. I’ve heard countless stories from our neighbors across this district who can’t get ahead no matter how hard they work, while politicians in Madison are playing political games and enriching their donors. Supporting working people around the state should not be partisan. It’s time to rebuild and restore a state government that serves our communities and the workers, small businesses and farms that keep this state running.
candidates.leg_q4: Conservation is deeply rooted in Wisconsin’s history. In the 1970s there was no wild turkey population in Wisconsin since their extirpation in the late 1800s. The Wisconsin DNR traded some ruffed grouse to Missouri for some of their wild turkey and in 1976 released 39 wild turkeys in the Driftless Area of SW Wisconsin. Today, WI hunters harvest around 50,000 turkeys annually. While the DNR has been stripped of scientists who make projects like this possible, I’m running to bring that conservation spirit back to Wisconsin.

candidates.name: Todd Novak
candidates.leg_q1: No response
candidates.leg_q2: No response
candidates.leg_q3: No response
candidates.leg_q4: No response

candidates.name: Nathan Tataje
candidates.leg_q1: Voters should cast their ballots based on a properly formed conscience, even if that means not voting for me. I would rather lose while upholding my genuine principles than win by compromising my ideals. In a race where every candidate claims to be an independent voice, only I have truly walked that path by foregoing the comforts of a partisan base. We must not allow candidates to pose as non-partisan populists while accepting funding from establishment party machines. The two-party system offers only two sides of the same coin. By running as a truly independent candidate, I demonstrate that every person in my district will be listened to sincerely. My sole motivation is the welfare of my constituents, not corporate PACs, lobbyists, or partisan agendas.
candidates.leg_q2: Sovereignty. Sovereignty in how our land is used, how are taxes are used (and collected), Sovereignty in how our municipalities operate, etc. To address these issues, I would work to repeal statist-based standards like Dillon's rule. I would also introduce and work toward legislation that allows for tax choice for a portion of the income taxes paid by individuals. Furthermore, I would fight for routine third-party/independent audits of all state/taxpayer funded agencies and departments, as well as require maximum transparency for legislators, beginning with closing the archaic loopholes that allow legislators to freely delete any and all records of communication, phone, email or otherwise.
candidates.leg_q3: Wisconsin government should operate on the principles of widespread economic ownership and true local control. The current two-party duopoly maintains a top-down funding model that prioritizes state-directed programs and corporate subsidies over the self-sufficiency of ordinary citizens. We must dismantle this centralized paradigm. Government should empower individual taxpayers by allowing them a direct say in how their state tax dollars are allocated to vital local services. Furthermore, the state must stop using eminent domain to seize private land for unregulated commercial developments, and instead invest in tools that turn wage earners into community equity owners. True solidarity means putting the homestead before the political machine.
candidates.leg_q4: Definitely the fact that the Green Bay Packers are the only community-owned, "nonprofit" franchise in the NFL. Although the NFL banned community ownership of NFL teams back in the 1960s, it didn't apply to Green Bay because they were community-owned long before these rules were enacted (community-owned since 1923 — almost 40 years prior to the 1960 rule change!) This exception of wide-ownership of an NFL team is even dubbed "The Green Bay Rule"!  (Although in the NFL bylaws it is officially titled Article V, Section 4.)

candidates.name: Lee Snodgrass
candidates.leg_q1: I’m a proven champion for my district and the Fox Cities. In my 5+ years in office I’ve gained the knowledge and built relationships with legislators on both sides of the aisle to solve problems and advance legislative solutions to improve the lives of constituents. I’ve earned the respect of community leaders and stakeholders that enable me to easily connect folks to the resources they need. This job requires a hardworking, accessible individual who will go to the mat for the people they represent. It requires nuance, compromise and the skill to navigate spaces where there are not always shared views. I’m adept and having these conversations and finding places of shared agreement where we can move forward on behalf of the people I represent.
candidates.leg_q2: The top issue is affordability. Whether it is the cost of gas, groceries, health care, child care, or housing, people are struggling. I’m a working class representative who holds two part time jobs in addition to my legislative job so I understand and have been part of authoring legislative solutions to help families reduce household expenses. From covering costs of prescription medications,  raising the state minimum wage, prpviding paid family leave, providing free school lunches, eliminating sales taxes on period products, reducing costs for renters, and state funding for public schools to keep property taxes in check, I will continue to work with my colleagues on ways the state can do its part to reduce costs and ensure all households can better make ends meet.
candidates.leg_q3: The biggest complaint voters have about government is how divided and contentious it has become. If we can agree on the problems, we should be able to work together in good faith on solutions, no matter the political affiliation. I have been recognized for my bipartisan efforts  and have authored several bills with Republicans. This should not be unusual. It should be the norm. We need to focus on our common love for Wisconsin and the people who call it home instead of fighting amongst ourselves.
candidates.leg_q4: Wisconsin as the "laboratory of democracy." I love that our state has historically led on equal rights and progressive policy. From the 1911 passage of the first workers compensation law to 1919 when we became the first state to ratify the 19th Amendment giving women the right to vote, Wisconsin has led. Unemployment compensation benefits,being the first to recognize collective bargaining rights for public employees, and our leadership on conservation and environmental policies, through the work of Gaylord Nelson are a few favorite facts of WI on the leading edge!

candidates.name: Reive Pullen
candidates.leg_q1: Voters in the district have made it very clear to me. They want a government that works and isn't filled with partisanship. As a United States Marine, small business owner, and former 911 dispatcher, I've spent my life dedicated to solving problems and serving the public. I'm new to politics and have no interest in partaking in the theatrics and posturing that is modern-day politics. While other candidates are running with the sole focus of putting their political party in the majority, my focus is on returning civility to politics and being respectful to everyone, so that once I'm elected, it won't matter which party is in the majority for me to be effective in representing the Fox Valley.
candidates.leg_q2: The school funding formula needs to be addressed, which will in turn help keep local property taxpayers from having to foot the bill every time the Appleton Area School District needs more money because we are getting less from the state in comparison to other districts. The funding formula was created in 1993, is overly complex, and has a lot of variables that need to be dialed in. Fixing this will be one of my top priorities upon being elected, and I will work to advocate for a simpler and more fair funding formula to ensure the Appleton Area School District is in a secure financial position for years to come.
candidates.leg_q3: The government needs to be effective while representing its citizens, which is why I believe it is in the best interest of the people of Wisconsin for their elected representatives to have a voice by allowing bills to be heard in committee, regardless of what party the author is in or who holds the majority. By the same token, I believe we need to get away from gerrymandering and continuously redistricting our maps. I have talked to many constituents who believe their representative is actually a neighboring representative because of how frequently our maps have changed in Wisconsin.
candidates.leg_q4: Right from my district, Appleton is home to one of the world's first-ever hydroelectric power plants, which was built in 1882 using a new generator system developed by Thomas Edison, and provided power to both homes and mills in the Fox Valley. That same drive to innovate is still a big part of what makes the Fox Valley special today.

candidates.name: Becky Nichols
candidates.elected_experience: Menasha City Council (2013-2025); Winnebago County Board (2022-2024)
candidates.leg_q1: I believe in a government that works for everyday people. I’m a problem solver working to improve people’s lives with real solutions rather than short-term fixes. Having served 12 years on the Menasha City Council, I’ve sat at countless kitchen tables and listened to people’s stories — their victories, their struggles, and their hopes. Those stories guided me in making decisions that helped people and strengthened our communities. Today, I hear stories about how families are struggling with rising costs from healthcare to groceries. We need a representative in Madison who is ready to roll up their sleeves and get to work to lower costs.
candidates.leg_q2: The cost of living is the top issue in my district. Working people deserve to be able to pay the bills, put food on the table, and have a little left over at the end of the week. The cost of everything is going up faster than wages. I’ll work to lower costs and make sure people don’t have to work multiple jobs to support their families.
candidates.leg_q3: For too long, Madison has been ignoring the needs of this community as families are struggling to make ends meet. I believe people want their government to work for them, and for their representatives to reach across the aisle to get things done. My accomplishments on the City Council and County Board were products of my collaborative approach, such as working to pass legislation making it achievable and affordable for families to remove lead pipes in Menasha. I want to take that approach to Madison and work for policies and investments that invest in people, families, communities.
candidates.leg_q4: America’s first kindergarten class was held in Watertown in 1856.

candidates.name: Rachael Dowling
candidates.leg_q1: For too long, we have watched the cost of everyday life rise while too many government decisions happen without enough public input, accountability, or common sense. I believe government should listen first, act responsibly, and reflect who it serves. That means standing up for working families, seniors, homeowners, small businesses, and everyone trying to build a stable life in our community. I’m not running to protect a political party. I’m running to protect the people who live here.
candidates.leg_q2:
The top issue in my community is the threat of data centers. As data centers and other large-scale developments expand, we must ask serious questions before moving forward:
• ​How much water will they use?
• How much electricity will they consume? 
• Who pays when demand increases?
• What safeguards are in place to protect residents from higher utility bills?
​Growth should not come at the expense of local families, small businesses, or our natural resources.​
candidates.leg_q3: Wisconsin government should operate with more transparency by making single-issue bills the standard. The failed $1.8 billion tax relief and school funding proposal is a good example. It combined school aid, special education funding, rebate checks, property tax cuts, and tax changes for tips and overtime into one package. Those issues deserved separate votes. When too much is bundled together, legislators are forced into all-or-nothing decisions, and voters lose clarity and the deserved relief to our communities. Single-issue bills create clear votes, stronger accountability, and better government.
candidates.leg_q4: Wisconsin packs more dairy cows into each square mile than any other state.

candidates.name: David Daniels
candidates.leg_q1: I believe strongly in service to the country. That's why I served in the Air Force. All of my experiences have prepared me to serve effectively. Starting a business, growing it, leading employees, balancing books, finding ways to save money and become more efficient are all experiences to help me succeed. As national president of AARST, I worked with different personalities and organizations to facilitate and accomplish goals. I’m level headed and I think before I speak. When it comes to making decisions, I ask other experts for counsel and form a decision. This new role will take a lot of work, which I’m prepared to do. I’m willing and able to work with my counterparts to make life better for constituents in my district.
candidates.leg_q2: The overwhelming response I have heard when meeting people and talking issues is "Please promise you will find a way to reduce my property taxes." And that is what I promise to do. We will look for ways to expand our housing base, increase tourism dollars and give back the state surplus to tax payers. When I accomplish that one thing for my district I will consider my first term a success.
candidates.leg_q3: We have to put Wisconsinites first and foremost, and be willing to work better together to help Wisconsin families. I am a family man with five kids. I know what it is like to struggle. No one gave me anything when starting out. I had to work two jobs, seven days a week to make ends meet. So, I know what it is like to struggle. Hard work is a good thing but families should be able to put some money away each month for retirement, emergencies, and some fun. We need to find a way to make living in Wisconsin and our district more affordable.
candidates.leg_q4: A piece of Sputnik, Russia's first satellite crashed onto a street in Manitowoc in 1962. To this day Manitowoc still celebrates with a party called Sputnikfest.

candidates.leg_q1: I have served the Oshkosh area reliably, responsibly and continue to focus on cost of living matters for the community.
candidates.leg_q2: Cost of public education, housing and healthcare.
candidates.leg_q3: Legislature, both houses, should work more towards making basic necessities and quality of life accessible and affordable for all of Wisconsin.
candidates.leg_q4: Lulu Shaw was Wisconsin’s first female mayor, elected in 1923 for Crandon, WI.

candidates.name: Alex Corrigan
candidates.leg_q1: I am running because I believe the people of the 55th District deserve a representative who is present, accessible, and focused on the realities of everyday life. Families across our communities are thinking about the cost of groceries, housing, childcare, healthcare, and whether opportunities will be available for the next generation. Those concerns deserve to be heard and taken seriously. I don’t have all the answers, but I am committed to listening, asking questions, and learning from the people who live and work here. My goal is to bring people together, focus on practical solutions, and represent the district with honesty, respect, and accountability. The job is not to serve a party — it is to serve the people of the 55th District.
candidates.leg_q2: Affordability is the issue that connects many of the concerns I hear across the 55th District. Families are worried about the rising costs of housing, childcare, healthcare, and everyday necessities. As a school board member, I also see how state funding decisions affect local taxpayers and community resources. Addressing affordability requires thoughtful investment, responsible budgeting, and policies that strengthen local communities rather than shifting costs onto families. I believe strong schools, economic opportunity, and responsible stewardship of taxpayer dollars go hand in hand. My approach would be to listen to residents, focus on practical solutions, and make sure state government is responsive to the real needs of the people it serves.
candidates.leg_q3: I think government works better when we stop treating people who disagree with us as enemies. Most people are trying to provide for their families, build a good life, and leave things a little better than they found them. I’d like to see more listening, more transparency, and more focus on solving problems instead of assigning blame. We won’t agree on everything, and that’s okay. But if we can’t even talk to each other, we can’t make good decisions together. Government should be a place where different perspectives are heard and where the focus stays on serving communities rather than serving political parties.
candidates.leg_q4: My favorite Wisconsin history story is the Sovereign State of Winneconne. After the village was accidentally left off the 1967 Wisconsin highway map, residents declared independence, talked about setting up toll booths, and launched a campaign to make sure they were noticed. The story is funny, which is part of why I love it. But what I find most interesting is what happened next. A community that felt ignored found a creative way to make its voice heard, and the conflict was ultimately resolved through comm cation and compromise rather than escalation. It’s a uniquely Wisconsin story — equal parts stubbornness, humor, civic engagement, and problem-solving.

candidates.name: Grace Abitz
candidates.leg_q1: I will be bold in speaking up for Assembly District 56. I want to introduce legislation that impacts people in a positive way. I want people to be empowered by their local and state government.
candidates.leg_q2: Public education funding and special education reimbursement rates are front of mind for the Hortonville Area School District. When we best serve students in public education, we are investing directly in kids and a more secure future for all. Legislators need to pass a budget that meets the needs of public education across the state.
candidates.leg_q3: There should be term limits on majority speakers.
candidates.leg_q4: Snowmobiles were invented in by Carl Eliason in Sayner, Wisconsin, in 1917.

candidates.name: Anthony W. Phillips
candidates.leg_q1: I have leadership experience as a cancer physician and in business. I've been medical director of a cancer clinic, overseeing 25 other providers of cancer care. I've successfully owned two businesses with as many as 120 employees. My conservative values fit well with the conservative nature of the 56th Assembly District. Though conservative, I do plan to work across the aisle on shared values such as first-time home ownership and improvement in reading/math/science scores in our public schools.
candidates.leg_q2: Affordability is the top issue in the 56th Assembly District. Rising property taxes is a common theme, in part from serial school and municipal referendums in the area. The public schools continue to want to increase their per-student spending, despite declining enrollment and declining performance scores. Reducing property taxes is an important way to increase the affordability of living in Wisconsin. Holding the line on state and national government spending in order to limit inflationary pressures will also improve affordability.  I'm personally interested in investing in our young, hard-working families, to help them afford their first home as a way of keeping them in the state.
candidates.leg_q3: The Wisconsin government is likely to be split in the near future, meaning neither major party is going to have complete power. There will have to be areas of compromise to finish state budgets, fund schools, have oversight of school performance, create an environment in Wisconsin positive for business development, etc. I am motivated to be a part of this discussion — I believe I can represent my conservative values but still find reasonable ways to invest in a positive future for our state.
candidates.leg_q4: The modern Republican Party was officially founded in Ripon, Wisconsin, on March 20, 1854, during an anti-slavery expansion meeting. The original GOP was on the right side of the Civil War! The lasting tenets of the Republican Party include small government, limit dependency on government, as reasonable today as they were in 1854. I've always been a Republican because of these basic values and will protect those values when I serve in Madison.

candidates.name: Shawna Riley
candidates.leg_q1: I am 51 years old, life hasn't been easy, l have experienced divorce, single mother, child with cancer, loss of jobs (plant closure) had to rely on badger care for a bit ,all these things have made me the woman qualified to do this job, l know struggle and what it's like to be one of the many working poor.
candidates.leg_q2: Taxes. l feel that we are over taxed, and now we have to pay for our water pipes to be replaced $4,000 even if it's spread out over four years is still a lot of money to a lot of people and especially after a flood and the damage that has caused. People simply are struggling to make ends meet.
candidates.leg_q3: We need to start taxing the wealthy and corporations, and fine anyone that has a negative effect on our natural resources, we also need to focus on better schools and healthy lunch programs. l'm hoping our farmers can help us with that.
candidates.leg_q4: I was told from one of the tour guide, that the woman on top of the Wisconsin state capital building was designed by the man that also designed the Lincoln memorial in Washington , l thought that was pretty cool.

candidates.name: Dylan Testin
candidates.leg_q1: I have been a voice and leader in my community long before running for office.
candidates.leg_q2: Cost of living and the tax burden is the easy answer, and is priority number 1 in my campaign, but we also need to focus on protecting our natural resources as they are a major contributor to our way of life in rural Wisconsin. From agriculture to tourism dollars, we rely heavily on our lakes and land in District 57.
candidates.leg_q3: Serving the people and the constituents of the state and government rather than catering to mega donors and PAC contributors. Too many partisan games are played and progress isn't being made to benefit Wisconsin residents.
candidates.leg_q4: Wisconsin holds the most festivals in the country, even though most of them are crammed into the summer and fall. From Summerfest to Old Fashioned Fest, there is something for everyone. It also shows our dedication as a state to the tourism industry that is unmatched anywhere else.

candidates.name: Bill Lorge
candidates.leg_q1: I was successful in the 1990s serving 10 years in the Assembly. My talents, experience and leadership can bring us all back together for the people of Wisconsin. I'm the best candidate to unite, not divide. I passed many great laws because I worked with both Republicans and Democrats like saving the Wolf River from the Exxon Mine, deregulating small rural cemeteries in Wisconsin, and making Highway 10 safer. My father was the senator from this district, so I learned well and became a leader. I retired from the corrupt dirty political world to raise my children, and I’m now able to get back to work to help save the world for them and future generations. Enough is enough, time to bring Bill back.
candidates.leg_q2: The Wolf River flooding. The Army Corps of Engineers need to dredge ditches to take the water so it does not flood our communities like it did again this year. I have a great history with the Wolf River, I love that river and will do all I can to solve this problem so our citizens can relax knowing that the flooding has finally been fixed.
candidates.leg_q3: Unity not divisive fighting among our elected officials. It's time to get the big money and corrupt politicians out of our government. Our politicians are bought and paid for by the greedy special interests and enough is enough. It's time to elect people like Bill Lorge who will vote in the Legislature to put the people back in power. Vote for the candidates who want to represent the people. Wisconsin was known as a good clean State regarding our government and our elected officials, but that era is long gone.  Time for a real change. Campaign finance laws need to be changed to get the dirty money out. I've seen it first hand and I know where to focus to win back our state.
candidates.leg_q4: "Fighting Bob" La Follette is someone I studied my whole life, and my family and the La Follette family were great friends, even in 1974 when my father Sen. Gerald Lorge and Bronson La Follette ran against each other for Wisconsin Attorney General. Later, in the 1990s I bought "Fighting Bob" La Follette's beautiful mahogany sideboard, which I still have today.

candidates.name: Ed Delgado
candidates.leg_q1: I am running for Wisconsin State Assembly because the people of the 57th District deserve a representative who will listen, show up, and fight for their interests. As a U.S. Marine Corps veteran, Waushara County Board supervisor, working professional, and longtime conservative advocate, I understand the challenges facing working families, small businesses, farmers, and communities throughout the district. I believe in limited government, fiscal responsibility, public safety, election integrity, constitutional carry, strong enforcement of immigration laws, lower taxes, and the protection of constitutional rights. Most importantly, I believe elected office should be earned through hard work and direct engagement with the people — not selected, but earned.
candidates.leg_q2: The number one issue I hear about across the 57th District is the rising cost of living. Families are paying more for groceries, gas, utilities, insurance, healthcare, and just about everything else they need to get by. At the same time, homeowners, farmers, retirees, and small business owners continue to feel the pressure of high property taxes and government spending. In our rural communities, people often have to drive long distances for work, school, appointments, and everyday errands, making higher fuel costs hit even harder. Working families are doing everything right, but many feel like they're falling further behind. That's why affordability, lower taxes, and responsible government spending aren't just political talking points—they're everyday concerns that directly impact the people of the 57th Assembly District.
candidates.leg_q3: I believe Wisconsin government needs to get back to common sense. The people of this state are tired of politicians talking at them instead of listening to them. Government should focus on its core responsibilities, spending taxpayer dollars wisely, protecting constitutional rights, supporting law enforcement, and creating opportunities for families, farmers, workers, and small businesses to succeed. Too often, government creates more bureaucracy and obstacles for the very people who are working hard to get ahead. I don't believe elected office should be about building a political career. It should be about showing up, listening, solving problems, and being accountable to the people who sent you there. Wisconsin deserves a government that works for the people.
candidates.leg_q4: Most people know Wisconsin as the Badger State, but did you know we're also the birthplace of one of the biggest internet horror phenomena in the world? Wisconsin earned its nickname in the 1820s and 1830s when lead miners dug shelters into hillsides and lived much like badgers. More recently, the famous image that inspired The Backrooms was traced to a building in Oshkosh, Wisconsin, where a photo taken during renovations in 2002 eventually became the foundation for a worldwide internet sensation. From hardworking miners living underground to the internet's most famous endless maze, Wisconsin has a history that's a little more interesting than most people realize.

candidates.name: Joey Marschall
candidates.leg_q1: I want to bring a voice to the regular working class people of our state. I want to make healthcare affordable for everyone and fix our public education funding to actually fund public schools in order to give our children to best opportunity for success and lower our property taxes. I also want to increase our minimum wage to a living wage.
candidates.leg_q2: I think affordability is the top issue. Some of the things I would do to address this is passing the Badgercare public option to help people afford healthcare. Also getting rid of the school voucher program, Public money should be going to public education and by funding public schools our property taxes dont have to continue to rise in order to pay for things the state should already be paying for.
candidates.leg_q3: Our government needs to focus more on the people and what it can do to help us all succeed and make life better for everyone. It needs to stop playing partisan games and work together to pass meaningful legislation to make Wisconsin thrive.

Republicans put the rich, wealthy individuals, large corporations and corporate farms first while mostly ignoring the needs of working people, middle class and family farms. As a credit union professional, I had a career fully following the founding principal and primary credit union tenet, people helping people. candidates.leg_q2: Funding public schools is becoming more difficult as money is diverted to charter schools. With higher income eligibility and statewide expansion, the state is now supporting two parallel school systems — an approach that is not sustainable. This is especially harmful to rural districts, which have fewer alternatives. Wisconsin’s school funding formula, largely unchanged since the 1990s, needs a major overhaul. Public schools also need more support for students with special needs, particularly because charter schools often do not serve those students.
candidates.leg_q3: While collecting signatures for nomination, I often heard why don't the two parties work together? I agree. Why? The people of Wisconsin cannot move forward when nothing is getting done. To do so, I will strive to find a way to compromise, finding common ground and understanding our opponents and constituents’ needs. We serve the people of Wisconsin, not the parties. Also, I will have regular in-district meetings to hear from constituents, not ducking doing so because there may be negative comments.
candidates.leg_q4: Once upon a time in a land named Wisconsin, margarin, called oleo in those days, was banned from being sold in the state. But it was smuggled in from Illinois on oleo runs by family and friends. My family couldn't afford butter and participated. Oleo was white and came in 8 oz pouches with yellow dye sacs to make it look like butter. As kids, we would fight to knead the bag turning the oleo yellow. And with family who were dairy farmers in the middle of the state, we could never tell them because oleo was forbidden, my first education on pressure. Today there is a similar situation with Spotted Cow runs to neighboring states since the beer is only sold in Wisconsin.

candidates.leg_q1: I'm an experienced local leader running as an independent candidate because I want to represent our district, not a political party. I was first elected to local office in 2021, and in just five years I've become a strong voice for Fond du Lac area residents. I work hard, I get to know the issues that matter to people, and I fight to find the best solutions that are practical and affordable. I'm not afraid to challenge the status quo when we deserve something better, and I look for ways to collaborate with others to make change happen. Right now we need major changes at the state level, and I am ready to get to work to help move Wisconsin forward.
candidates.leg_q2: Education funding and the property tax impact is the top issue in my district. Both the Fond du Lac and North Fond du Lac School Districts have seen two operational referendum attempts fail in recent years. Many voters have said they simply cannot afford to raise their own property taxes when the cost of living keeps rising. We need to support our public schools, while taking pressure off property taxpayers. Wisconsin needs to change the school funding formula so that school districts receive more state aid. We need to find a sustainable funding source, much like the legislature did in the recent change to the shared revenue formula, which tied state shared revenue to a percentage of the state sales tax.
candidates.leg_q3: We need to be proactive, not reactive. When it comes to issues like education and child care, we're really at a tipping point. If we don't make some major systemic changes, we are going to see school districts go bankrupt and child care will only be accessible to the wealthiest families. We're letting huge AI data centers come in and secure themselves sweet deals, while residents worry about land and water use and rising energy costs. And all of this is happening while the cost of everything keeps going up. Wisconsin residents feel like no one is looking out for them. We need leaders in the legislature who will take control and make plans that lead to a better future for our state.
candidates.leg_q4: Fond du Lac was almost the state capital! In 1836 when Wisconsin was a newly formed territory, Fond du Lac was in a tight race with Madison to be named the territory's capital, and Fond du Lac lost by only one vote.

candidates.name: Marty Ryan
candidates.elected_experience: Fond du Lac City Council (1999-2005), president (2000-2004); Fond du Lac County Board (2014-present), first vice-chair
candidates.leg_q1: I believe all governments should be efficient, accountable, and focused on real results — not empty promises. My record speaks for itself: smart solutions, fiscal responsibility, working together, and a commitment to strengthening the community.  I have the experience that  Assembly representatives need to hit the ground running on day one. Just as I've done on the FDL City Council and county board, Now, I'm ready to bring that same leadership to the state Assembly.
candidates.leg_q2: Fiscal management — government should live within its means — just like families do. I'm committed to cutting waste, improving efficiency, and making sure taxpayer dollars are spent wisely. With a proven track record of reducing waste and improving services, I'm able to bring practical, results-driven leadership to ensure government works better for everyone. People in this state are hurting financially, I'm committed to lower income and property taxes and finding the waste and abuse in our state government and holding those responsible for it accountable.
candidates.leg_q3: 1) We have to get our local property taxes in line. My first job on day one is repealing the Gov. Evers 400 year veto. 2) The state school funding formula is broken and need to be torn apart and rebuilt.
candidates.leg_q4: The name Fond du Lac is French for "bottom of the lake." Early French explorers gave our community this name because it sits at the southern tip of Lake Winnebago. For centuries, this area served as an important crossroads for Native American tribes, fur traders, and settlers traveling through what would become Wisconsin. Today, Fond du Lac continues to be a gateway to Lake Winnebago and one of Wisconsin's great communities. Fond du Lac was also once known as the "Railroad City" of Wisconsin. By the late 1800s, multiple rail lines converged here, helping transform the city into a major manufacturing and transportation hub for the state.

candidates.name: Ben Brist
candidates.leg_q1: Wisconsin families are being squeezed. Property taxes, groceries, rent, childcare, healthcare… the basics keep getting more expensive while wages struggle to keep up. I’m running because our district deserves a representative who actually feels that pressure, not one who’s insulated from it. I grew up in a family that depended on public sector work, and I served in the military where I learned to lead and find common ground with people who see the world differently than I do. That’s the experience I’ll bring to Madison. In the Assembly, I’ll cut through the noise and focus on what matters: lowering costs for working families, protecting good jobs, and making sure every kid gets a quality education. I’m ready to fight for you.
candidates.leg_q2: Talk to almost any homeowner in this district and you’ll hear the same frustration: property taxes keep climbing, and it never feels like enough. That’s what happens when the state chronically underfunds public education and shifts the burden onto local communities. I’ve seen firsthand that a good education opens doors. Every kid in Wisconsin deserves that, regardless of their zip code. In the Assembly, I’ll fight to fix the state funding formula so local schools get what they need without hammering property owners.
candidates.leg_q3: Republican leadership in Madison has ignored what families in this district already know: the cost of living is crushing people. Groceries, property taxes, healthcare, etc. Things keep getting harder, and the legislature keeps looking the other way. This has to change. Wisconsin government should work for the people paying the bills, not the special interests funding campaigns. It should be responsive, honest, and willing to make tough calls even when it’s uncomfortable.
candidates.leg_q4: Wisconsin led the nation on labor rights as we were the first state to pass a public employee collective bargaining law in 1959!

candidates.name: Brian Bock
candidates.leg_q1: I am running to represent Assembly District 61 to deliver practical, results-driven leadership for every resident — today and for future generations. As school board treasurer, I helped uphold our commitment to not raise the tax levy while maintaining strong educational outcomes. I am a community advocate focused on addressing family costs, supporting high-quality schools, and improving access to healthcare. I am also an active volunteer, often found at community events, coaching youth, and supporting my children’s activities. I am committed to responsible governance, fiscal accountability, and building a stronger, more affordable District 61 for all.
candidates.leg_q2: Affordability is the top issue in our district, and working families need real relief now. I would address this by making sure we use the tax dollars we already collect more wisely, cutting wasteful spending, and prioritizing essential services that directly support our schools and communities. We should make every dollar count so taxpayers are not forced to cover extra costs just to keep community services functioning. By optimizing spending and focusing on what truly matters, we can protect public resources, strengthen local services, and reduce the financial burden on Wisconsinites. Responsible budgeting is not about doing less for our communities — it is about doing better with the resources we already have.
candidates.leg_q3: Wisconsin government should embrace a new Wisconsin Forward ideal — one that ensures government works for every resident. We must prioritize sustainable, commonsense policies that support people at every stage of life, from our youngest to our oldest. That means strengthening education, expanding access to healthcare, and supporting both rural and urban communities alike. Just as importantly, the legislature and governor must work together and listen to one another — regardless of party — to deliver real results. When we come together around shared goals and practical solutions, we can create opportunity and stability across our state and ensure every Wisconsinite has the chance to thrive.
candidates.leg_q4: Colby cheese is a classic American cheese that began in Colby, Wisconsin, where Joseph F. Steinwand, at 16 years old, developed it in 1885. He created it at his family’s cheese factory by washing the curds with cold water, which made the cheese milder, moister, and softer than cheddar. The town of Colby gave the cheese its name, and it quickly became known as one of Wisconsin’s signature dairy products. Colby’s success shows Wisconsin’s strong 19th-century cheesemaking tradition that continues to today. Colby remains closely tied to Wisconsin’s dairy heritage and history.

candidates.leg_q1: I’m running for state Assembly because Milwaukee’s southwest suburbs deserve a representative who will fight for them. Families across our community deserve a leader focused on solutions, not political drama. I’m running to bring real world experience to Madison and fight for affordable healthcare, strong public schools, safer neighborhoods, and an economy that gives everyone a fair opportunity to succeed.
candidates.leg_q2: The top issue facing our district is affordability. Too many families are struggling with rising housing costs, healthcare expenses, childcare bills, and property taxes while wages have failed to keep pace. Seniors worry about being priced out of the communities they helped build, and young families are finding it harder to buy a home and raise children. I will focus on practical solutions that lower costs for working families by expanding affordable housing, increasing access to quality childcare, protecting and improving access to healthcare and mental health services, and fully funding public education to reduce the burden on local property taxpayers. Wisconsin families deserve policies that make it easier to build financial stability, achieve homeownership, and remain in the communities they proudly call home.
candidates.leg_q3: For the past 20 years Wisconsin government has been run from the top down, with decisions being made behind closed doors by a small group of political insiders. Under Robin Vos and the current legislative leadership, we’ve seen political power take priority over solving real problems working families are facing. It’s time for a government that is more transparent, accountable, and focused on results. That means bringing more voices to the table, not just lobbyists, and political insiders, but working families, small business owners, educators, and community leaders. Everyone deserves a seat at the table and a voice in decisions that affect their lives.  Wisconsin works best when we focus on common-sence solutions, respect different perspectives, and put people ahead of politics.
candidates.leg_q4: One of my favorite Wisconsin fun facts is that Earth Day was founded here by Sen. Gaylord Nelson. He recognized that protecting our environment is about more than preserving natural beauty. It is about protecting our health, economy, and future generations. That lesson remains just as important today. Wisconsin's lakes, rivers, parks, and outdoor spaces are among our greatest treasures, but they face challenges from pollution and climate change. We have a responsibility to protect these resources and leave them better than we found them. Earth Day reminds us that Wisconsin has a proud conservation legacy. We should continue that tradition by investing in clean water, protecting our natural resources, and advancing practical environmental solutions so future generations can enjoy the Wisconsin we love.

candidates.name: Mike Bellagio
candidates.leg_q1: I am interested in observing substantive change. As a parent, I am concerned about the current trajectory of our nation and believe it is imperative to re-establish fundamental family values.
candidates.leg_q2: Regarding education, it is imperative that we reflect on past educational methodologies that fostered a robust learning environment for our children. I advocate for the reintroduction of traditional textbooks and comprehensive writing assignments. candidates.leg_q3: The extent of government intervention in the lives of American citizens has become excessive. It is imperative to streamline operations, eliminate waste and fraudulent activities, and reallocate funds to the residents of Wisconsin.
candidates.leg_q4: In 1922, Stephen Poplawski, an inventor based in Racine, Wisconsin, pioneered the integration of rotating blades at the base of a container. His initial intent was to facilitate the blending of soda fountain malted milks, thereby creating what is now recognized as the kitchen blender.

candidates.name: Angelina M. Cruz
candidates.leg_q1: Voters who reside in Assembly District 62 should elect me because I have deep roots in Racine — born and raised here, and committed to building my professional life here throughout my adult years. I understand both the challenges our community faces and the tremendous opportunities we have to grow. My experience as an educator and labor leader has given me the skills to bring together people of diverse backgrounds and perspectives to accomplish shared goals, even across differences. As a freshman legislator, I have carried that commitment into my work on the Education and Government Operations, Accountability, and Transparency (GOAT) Committees, focusing on strengthening public school funding, supporting students and educators, and restoring the dignity and respect that working people and labor deserve.
candidates.leg_q2: A top issue in our district is wage stagnation alongside rapidly rising costs of living. Racine residents earn roughly 30% below the state average income — Wisconsin's minimum wage has remained frozen at $7.25 per hour since 2009. That's why I introduced legislation this session to raise the state minimum wage to a living wage: increasing to $15 upon enactment, then rising $1.25 annually until reaching $20 per hour in 2030, after which it would be indexed to inflation. The bill raises the tipped wage to 50% of the minimum wage, includes a gradual phase-in for small businesses with 50 or fewer employees, and restores local control so communities may set higher standards. Higher wages strengthen purchasing power and boost state income tax revenue.
candidates.leg_q3: For decades, Wisconsin government has been entrenched in one-party control unresponsive to the will of its people. As one of the most gerrymandered states in the nation, Wisconsin has long denied its citizens fair representation — but newly redrawn maps give us the opportunity to elect legislators who truly reflect the values and aspirations of our communities. The Wisconsin Idea holds that state government should serve as a laboratory of democracy, where the boundaries of the Capitol extend to every corner of the state. That means drawing on a diversity of perspectives, engaging in constructive dialogue, and forging compromise in the genuine interest of constituents -- not party or power.
candidates.leg_q4: Wisconsin was the first state to recognize collective bargaining rights for public employees — a proud legacy that made the 2011 assault on those rights all the more an egregious provocation. When Gov. Walker introduced Act 10, stripping most public workers of collective bargaining, tens of thousands flooded the Capitol in one of the largest protest movements in modern state history. As a public school teacher, I was among them. That attack on my rights as a worker activated me politically in a way nothing else had. It set me on a path of advocacy and civic engagement that ultimately led me to serve as the president of my local union and in the legislature to protect and restore the rights and dignity of working people.

candidates.leg_q2: Affordability is the issue. People are working hard, but the basics cost too much: housing, healthcare, groceries, utilities, and property taxes. And with a pro-worker, pro-public education, pro-healthcare majority in Madison, we can finally move the backlog of strong bills that lower costs, protect rights, and make government work for working families again.

Raise the minimum wage. To support these and other changes that would actually help Wisconsinites, I support the creation of a large, sustainable tax revenue through a wealth tax and the legalization of cannabis.
candidates.leg_q3: The word FORWARD is on our flag, yet the current leadership has done little in the way of progress. We need to stop regressing and start living up to Wisconsin's state motto.
candidates.leg_q4: The first commercial typewriter was invented in Wisconsin.

candidates.name: Jeff Disher
candidates.leg_q1: No response
candidates.leg_q2: No response
candidates.leg_q3: No response
candidates.leg_q4: No response

candidates.name: Vinnie Miresse
candidates.elected_experience: Wisconsin State Assembly (2025-present); Portage County Board (2017-2026)
candidates.leg_q1: I am running for re-election to the Wisconsin state Assembly because I believe that good politics should be a vehicle for improving people’s lives. At a time of rising costs for groceries, fuel, and healthcare, and increasing skepticism regarding the role of government, my goal remains to inspire optimism. I am committed to leading with fierce compassion, driving meaningful change, and delivering tangible results for the people of central Wisconsin.
candidates.leg_q2: The cost of living has become unsustainable. From food and gas to healthcare and energy, prices are rising at an alarming rate. Everyday citizens are unfairly bearing the financial burden of federal policy failures, international conflicts, and corporate interests. The people of the 71st District deserve an economic system that is fair, just, and inclusive of everyone, not just a privileged few. We are seeking the opportunity to earn an honest living in safe, healthy, and supportive communities where we can provide for our families and enjoy a good quality of life.
candidates.leg_q3: Government should work for the people. For the past 15 years, Wisconsin has been under one-party control, and their hyper-partisan, failed leadership has adversely impacted our state. We live in a purple state with a culture of "can-do" folks who bring a diversity of skills, perspectives, and ideas to the table. Our constituents expect us to achieve results despite our political differences. Wisconsinites want bipartisanship. They are tired of the culture wars, bickering, and the "gotcha" mentality; they simply want the legislature to get to work and deliver results that will make their lives better.
candidates.leg_q4: Wisconsin is a state of many "capitals," which reinforces our "can-do" Wisconsin work ethic and pride in our craft, products, industriousness, and sense of place. We are home to the Beer Capital of the World, Bratwurst Capital of the World, Cranberry Capital of the World, Toilet Paper Capital of the World, Ginseng Capital of the World, Troll Capital of the World, Snowmobile Capital of the World, Loon Capital of the World, and even the UFO Capital of the World. Of course, Wisconsin is also the Cheese Capital of the World. While we proclaim these titles with pride, we do so with a deep sense of "Midwest nice" and the kind of self-deprecating humor that only a cheesehead can truly understand.

candidates.name: Scott Krug
candidates.elected_experience: Wisconsin State Assembly (2011-present); Adams County Board (2022-2025); Tri Lakes Management District (3 years)
candidates.leg_q1: Voters should elect me because I have a proven record of showing up, listening, and delivering results for central Wisconsin. As a lifelong resident of the district, I understand our communities because I live here too. No one keeps the needs of the 72nd District top of mind more than I do, and the local wins we’ve achieved together prove it. Whether it’s protecting taxpayers, supporting local schools, preserving jobs, securing investments in our communities, improving election integrity, or expanding housing opportunities, I’ve focused on practical solutions rather than partisan talking points. I believe elected officials should be accessible, honest, and accountable. My goal has always been simple: leave our communities stronger and more affordable for the next generation.
candidates.leg_q2: The top issue in my district is affordability. Families are paying more for groceries, housing, utilities, and property taxes, while many feel their paychecks simply don’t go as far as they used to. Wisconsin has a significant budget surplus, and I believe a portion of that money should be returned to taxpayers while also investing in long-term solutions. That means property tax relief, reducing the tax burden on working families, increasing housing supply, and ensuring energy policies don’t drive up utility bills. We also need to continue growing family-supporting jobs so people can build a future here. Government should help make life more affordable, not make it harder to get ahead.
candidates.leg_q3: Wisconsin government needs to get back to solving problems instead of managing them. Families don’t care which party gets credit — they care whether they can afford groceries, pay their property taxes, find housing, and build a future here. Quite simply, our taxes are still too damn high. We should use government to create opportunity, not dependency, and measure success by results, not rhetoric. That means responsible budgeting, returning excess tax dollars when possible, investing in long-term economic growth, and giving local communities a stronger voice in decisions that affect them. Government won’t solve every problem, but it should stop creating new ones.
candidates.leg_q4: One of my favorite Wisconsin history facts is that Chief Oshkosh, the Menominee leader for whom the City of Oshkosh is named, was born near Point Basse along the Wisconsin River in what is now the 72nd Assembly District. During the 1800s, he helped lead the Menominee through a difficult period of treaty negotiations and fought to keep his people in Wisconsin when many Native American tribes were being forced west. Because of his leadership, the Menominee remain one of the few tribes that retained a permanent homeland in their ancestral state. It’s a fascinating reminder that some of Wisconsin’s most important history happened right here along the Wisconsin River long before our modern cities existed.

candidates.name: Christine Maltese
candidates.leg_q1: I may be new to politics, but I'm not new to solving problems, working hard, and listening to people. I see being new as an advantage because I'm not coming in with years of political baggage or obligations. My focus is on the people of the 72nd District. I want to hear their concerns, understand their challenges, and make sure their voices are represented in Madison. At the end of the day, this campaign isn't about politics — it's about people.
candidates.leg_q2: The issues I hear about most often are property taxes, access to healthcare, and the rising cost of everyday life. Families are working hard, yet many feel like they are falling further behind as housing, childcare, groceries, insurance, and utilities continue to increase. Rural communities are also concerned about keeping local schools strong and ensuring healthcare remains available close to home. As someone who is new to politics, I spend more time listening than talking. What I hear is that people are tired of political talking points and want practical solutions that make life more affordable and strengthen our communities. My focus will be on representing the voices of the people of the 72nd District and bringing their concerns directly to Madison.
candidates.leg_q3: Wisconsin has changed over the years, and too often decisions have been driven by political agendas rather than the needs of the people who live and work here. I believe that can be changed when elected officials spend less time listening to party leaders and special interests and more time listening to their constituents. Government works best when it is accountable, transparent, and focused on solving real problems. The people of Wisconsin deserve representatives who are willing to have honest conversations, consider different perspectives, and put communities ahead of politics. Change begins when voters elect leaders who remember that they work for the people — not the other way around.
candidates.leg_q4: One of my favorite Wisconsin history facts is that before becoming famous for dairy farming, parts of Wisconsin were known for lead mining. In fact, Wisconsin's nickname, "The Badger State," comes from miners who dug into hillsides and sometimes lived in those tunnels, much like badgers.

candidates.name: Frank Kostka
candidates.leg_q1: I was born and raised in Ashland and served 20 years in the Air Force. My time in the service took me across the country but I always felt Ashland was my home and spent most of my vacations here. My northern Wisconsin values attracted me to come back home to Ashland where I opened a small business. I feel the leadership and problem-solving experience I developed in the military would be an asset representing northern Wisconsin in Madison. As a business owner, I listened to customers complaining about housing, taxes, utility costs, lack of jobs and government spending, but all I could do was share their concerns. As a representative I would continue to listen to our citizens’ concerns and voice them in Madison.
candidates.leg_q2: The big concerns in the district are high taxes, energy costs and job opportunities. I would encourage our legislature to be fiscally responsible and thereby reduce the tax burden. Support the development and improvements of our energy infrastructure. Job opportunities in Northern Wisconsin have always been lacking, that’s one of the reasons I left the area to join the military. Many of our jobs up north are service oriented, but it’s hard to raise a family or buy a house with only that income. I would promote the benefits of our area to encourage businesses with good paying jobs to move up north and at the same time support existing companies to expand.
candidates.leg_q3: Wisconsin is eighth highest in the country on property taxes, so we’re being overtaxed. This is exemplified by the current $1.8 billion budget surplus, and they are debating how to spend it or to refund it back to the people they took it from. If I had a personal budget and end up with extra money, I would put it in my savings account and not find some frivolous way to spend it, but I guess that’s just me and my conservative values. For me if the state has more money than budgeted for, it should be returned to the taxpayers. I would be fiscally responsible in evaluating funding programs that are necessary to run our state.
candidates.leg_q4: I love our Wisconsin state flag because it describes the strength and history of our state. But some items on the flag that were significant to our economy in the past are no longer viable due to political unpopularity. For example, the crossed pick and shovel for mining and a pyramid of pig lead, symbolizing abundance and mineral wealth are almost non-existent today.

candidates.name: Angela Stroud
candidates.leg_q1: I am proud of what I accomplished in my first term: from securing a deal that ensured that lead line replacement in Superior would cost residents zero dollars, to authoring a data center regulation bill that is being considered a model for other states, I spent this year working as hard as I could for the people I represent. I believe that the role of government is to protect the people from corporate and elite power, and to help solve problems that can’t be solved by individuals alone, like funding public schools and securing access to quality, affordable healthcare, housing, and childcare. My focus is on making government more effective so that it can help people and communities thrive.
candidates.leg_q2: Though there are many issues to address in the 73rd, the most central problem is the cost of living, in particular housing. From property taxes to a lack of adequate supply, there is a broad array of issues that affect housing costs. Property taxes have increased in part because the state has failed to uphold its end of the bargain in funding public schools. We solve this by ensuring that general aids and special education reimbursements meet our constitutional obligations with state money so that local residents are only paying their fair share. As for building more units, we need to find ways to bring down costs by coordinating across units of government, subsidizing development, and supporting our local supply chains.
candidates.leg_q3: We need to be more focused on getting results for people, not special-interest groups or wealthy donors.
candidates.leg_q4: I love that the Anishinaabe people found their way to these lands following a prophecy that told them to go to where food grows on water. Our ecosystems provide us with incredible gifts for survival and a ton of opportunity to have fun outside. We owe it to ourselves and to the planet to respect, honor, and protect those gifts, and the Anishinaabe prophecy reminds us of that fact.

candidates.name: Scott Harbridge
candidates.occupation: Former Wisconsin Department of Corrections officer
candidates.leg_q1: I’m a veteran, retired Wisconsin Corrections Sergeant, Christian, fiscal conservative, husband, father, and grandfather. I’ve dedicated my life to serving others. During my career with the Department of Corrections, I served on the Policies & Procedures Committee, led an Emergency Response Unit team, and represented fellow officers in grievance proceedings. I’ve volunteered as a driver for Camp Douglas Rescue, where I earned EVOC and CPR certifications. I’ve served as vice president of a women's pro-life resource center and vice president of WRA — an Alliance for Life, Liberty & Justice — and am currently an ambassador for Shepherd's Watch Foundation. I’ll always stand for life, liberty, election integrity, lower taxes, responsible government spending, and putting service before politics. I’m a proven conservative leader who serves people, not special interests.
candidates.leg_q2: As a resident of Wisconsin's North Woods, I am especially concerned about proposals that place additional fees on outdoor recreation. The North Woods is one of Wisconsin's greatest treasures. Families come here to hike, kayak, bicycle, ski, camp, fish, and enjoy God's creation. Tourism supports local businesses, restaurants, lodging facilities, and jobs. We should be encouraging people to visit and enjoy Wisconsin—not create new barriers and new fees that make recreation more expensive, for vacationers and local families alike. Caring for our natural resources is equally important, teaching our youth the importance of conservation, responsible, safe hunting and fishing ensures these resources are available for generations to come.
candidates.leg_q3: We need to eliminate waste in government. 1. Every department should be able to find at least 10% minimum deduction of waste in their budget. 2. Every organization, that tax payer money is allocated to, needs to be independently audited. 3. Every department; for example the DNR needs to pass a real independent audit, any missing funds or miss-allocated funds, properly investigated so there can be accountability. 4. Streamline departments, cutting needless positions that repeat responsibilities, and are layered in bureaucracy.
candidates.leg_q4: Wisconsin has more than 15,000 lakes, actually more than Minnesota. The over 160 different species of fish that we have in our state is a fisherman's dream. We also have thousands of miles of rivers and streams in our state. The Fresh Water Fishing Hall of Fame is located in Hayward, also in the 74th Assembly District. One of America's favorite past times is fishing and we need to support stocking and protecting this valuable resource.

candidates.occupation: Tavern owner; utilities manager; state representative
